I find it bizarre that they felt the need to specify "Asian". What does that have to do with anything?
Latin alphabet transcription of East Asian languages tend to be incredibly lossy and there tends to be a lot of ambiguities.

That Vietnamese surname of Nguyen is formally written as Nguyễn in the current script, or as 阮 in the old adapted Hanzi script, and practically pronounced somewhere around "gwen". Most other EA countries tend to do equivalents of "阮" -> "gwen", and East Asian cultures generally prefer Last-First ordering, which tend to put more information in the first name, and so there are going to be tons of last names in Latin that end up being barely unambiguous to be a form of identification.

These can be a problem if email addresses are going to be formulated as e.g. "阮 必成" -> "Nguyễn Tất Thành" -> "Gwen Tat Than" -> "t.gwen@example.net", even if the surname is going to be that much long(although Nguyen in particular is just identical even in Vietnamese).

(Japan may be less affected thanks to having default 2+ char random surnames farmers made up in modernization efforts, but there are still the 灘(nada) highscool, the 津(tsu) city, etc etc that can be NLP problems)
Yes, but why specify it? Why not just say „they confused 2 people with the same name“? Adding „Asian“ doesn’t add anything to the story other than flagging Apple as casually racist

Even if Westerners maintained the characters for the names rather than transliterate them, there's still the problem that common surnames are used by literally hundreds of millions of people of Chinese descent, and there are a lot of commonly-used given names as well. I think in all of Chinese, Korean, and Vietnamese almost all given names are 1-2 syllables in length, so there's even less space for disambiguation, even before you get to the additionally ambiguities introduced by transliteration and dropping of diacritics.
Japanese has several advantages:
1. Both given names and surnames often use more than 2 syllables. This makes it more familiar to speakers of European languages, where multi-syllable words are no big deal.
2. English speakers find Japanese easier to pronounce and remember due to its simpler syllable structure and use of globally more common sounds compared to the other languages.
3. Unlike the other languages, Japanese names are always given in Given Name, Surname order in English media, while names from the other languages are inconsistently transcribed in either order.

4. Japanese is the "default" East Asian culture for the West in many ways, since it's the one that at least the US has most deeply engaged for the longest time. Many, many cultural exports that actually originated in China were introduced to the West via Japan with Japanese names. Also, Japan has been an advanced industrial economy since the late 1800s, while China only achieved that status a few decades ago.

5. Japanese transcription into Roman characters has remained consistent for a long time (helped by the simpler phonology). Chinese and Korean have been cursed with several incompatible transcription systems over the years - although Pinyin has been winning out for Chinese, there are still many names with legacy transcriptions, not to mention the other Chinese languages needing their own transcriptions. Vietnamese does exclusively use Latin characters, but the diacritics and unfamiliar pronunciation makes them harder to remember.

Reading through this, the Apple side of the story is actually the more fascinating one. It's frankly bizarre that a company of that scale had to rely on a former employee's (Chang Liu) personal iCloud access. Combine that with their legal team confusing an Asian surname and emailing the wrong person, and publicly, Apple just ends up looking incompetent and deceitful.

By choosing to release these receipts to the public instead of saving them for court, OpenAI is executing a very deliberate PR strategy. They are effectively framing Apple as a sloppy, legacy company. As with most corporate litigation PR, information is selectively released. Here, OpenAI is trying to reframe Apple's own operational failures as the root cause, rather than any actual technology theft by OpenAI.
Looking at the bigger picture, it's clear who is actually at a disadvantage: OpenAI.

Whether Apple's tech was copied or not is almost secondary. The real existential threat for OpenAI is the legal discovery process, which could expose their internal AI architecture and training data to the public (and to Apple). That risk is exactly why OpenAI is playing this out in the court of public opinion—to force Apple's hand.

Ultimately, both sides have a lot to lose. Apple has always marketed itself on 'privacy, security, and perfection,' but this incident pulls back the curtain on how sloppy their internal operations can be. OpenAI has their own black boxes to protect. In the end, this isn't about truth; it's a pure media management war to see who blinks first.

东亚语言的拉丁字母转写往往会丢失大量信息，并且往往存在很多歧义。
越南姓氏 Nguyen 在现行文字中正式写为 Nguyễn，或在旧有的汉字书写中写为“阮”，实际发音大约类似于“gwen”。大多数其他东亚国家倾向于有类似于“阮”->“gwen”的对应发音，而且东亚文化通常偏好姓在前名在后的顺序，这往往会在名字中包含更多信息，因此会有大量拉丁字母拼写的姓氏最终几乎无法明确作为身份识别的依据。

日语有几个优势：
1. 名字和姓氏通常都包含2个以上的音节。这让欧洲语言的使用者感到更熟悉，因为在他们的语言中多音节词是很平常的事。
2. 英语使用者觉得日语更容易发音和记忆，因为与其他语言相比，日语的音节结构更简单，且使用了在全球范围内更常见的发音。
3. 与其他语言不同，在英语媒体中，日语姓名总是按照“名、姓”的顺序排列，而其他语言的姓名在音译时的顺序则并不统一。
4. 在许多方面，日本是西方眼中的“默认”东亚文化，因为至少对美国而言，它是接触时间最长、程度最深的文化。许多实际上起源于中国的文化输出，都是通过日本以日本名称传入西方的。此外，自19世纪末以来，日本一直是一个先进的工业经济体，而中国直到几十年前才达到这一地位。
5. 日语罗马音的转写方式长期以来保持一致（这也得益于其更简单的语音系统）。多年来，中文和韩文一直受困于几种互不兼容的转写系统——尽管 Pinyin 在中文转写中逐渐占据主导地位，但仍有许多姓名保留着旧式的转写方式，更不用说其他汉语变体还需要各自的转写系统。越南语确实完全使用拉丁字母，但其变音符号和陌生的发音方式让人更难记住。

哦，这是在公司发放的设备上操作的，我没有保留源代码！我只是解释一下这可能是本应触发调查但并没有的事情。
在过去，开发人员保留源代码之类的东西曾经是很常见的事。
我记得实习期间有一位经理告诉我写整洁的代码，因为以后我可能需要在未来的工作经验中复用部分代码。那还是用 zip 之类的方式或网络共享来分享代码的时代。
那时候并没有那么多“软件作坊”，这只是在其他公司（比如硬件制造商）做事的一种方式。显然，你会被信任不会带走、传播或复用公司的商业机密或类似的东西，这本来也是你合同中竞业禁止条款所期望的。
从那以后，很多公司变得像“软件生产”公司，开发人员现在被视为像工厂工人一样。
在某种程度上，我想说如今你的代码被剥夺了，甚至连署名都没有了。
听着，在80/90年代，了解大公司主要开发者的名字是很常见的，而且他们的贡献也会明确归功于他们。但现在你几乎很难知道任何东西的代码是哪个开发者写的。高层管理者/架构师/...可能为人所知，但并不是因为他们的代码贡献。
你说得太对了，我完全忘了复用通用函数、类和工厂模式曾经是多么理所当然的事。我想归根结底，多亏了 LLM，这一切最终都变得毫无价值了。
我确实记得我们部门的首席工程师在最后一天上班时带了个硬盘来。就是那些能访问国家数据库，以及影响全国大部分人口的生产系统的人。这种事在今天根本不可能发生。
尽管我不是那种处理 PCB 原理图或最前沿 IP 的人。
这种不专业的博客式咆哮怎么会出现在 OpenAI 的网站上？这难道不应该在两家公司之间解决，而不是试图利用舆论法庭吗？
此外，我完全不知道这是怎么回事，也不知道我是否应该关心。
任何有自尊心的律师通常都会让你闭嘴，不要发这种东西。法官不喜欢媒体审判。
我认为他们希望对 Elon 用过的招数对 Apple 也能奏效。
哎呀。大写的哎呀。这只会更清楚地表明 Altman 实际上有多么软弱。
感觉就像他们想获得近20年前 Jobs 那篇《关于 Flash 的思考》所得到的同样影响力，并认为 ChatGPT 能做得更好。
律师是不会建议发布这个的。
退一步讲，这个案件绝对指出了 Apple 在 iOS 多用户功能方面做出的各种架构决策的缺陷。
Apple 在其人力资源实践中不区分个人账户和企业账户，这非常可疑。一个多用户操作系统为了在这个意义上卖出更多硬件而被阉割，也相当可悲。
我不明白的是，如果两家公司处于法律纠纷中，他们可以通过发博客文章或分享除了发布方之外无人验证的证据来讨论案件并试图影响公众舆论吗？
OpenAI 即使在筹集了这么多资金之后，也从未预料到会发生这样的事情，却还在继续自掘坟墓。
事已至此，他们剩下的只有妥协并付钱，否则他们就完了。
Apple 对阵 OpenAI 将是一场关于传承、信任和创新的战争。
> OpenAI 即使在筹集了这么多资金之后，也从未预料到会发生这样的事情，却还在继续自掘坟墓。
狂妄自大。
OpenAI 总是有选择将自己转变为一个我称之为“国家安全公司”的选项。
我的意思是，看看 Kim Dotcom 或 Aaron Schwartz 就知道了。
> 他们可以通过发博客文章或分享除了发布方之外无人验证的证据来讨论案件并试图影响公众舆论吗？
在 Trump 时代，一切皆有可能
对我来说，这看起来像是 OpenAI 感到恐惧，并试图在公众舆论中抢占先机以控制话语权。真是个垃圾公司。
他们把整个商业模式建立在窃取的数据上，当另一家公司对他们毫无信任时却装作很惊讶。
根据他们的过往记录，这场诉讼一点也不出人意料。
是的，根据他们的一贯表现（我是说，现在连他们的名字都成了一个烂笑话），我不倾向于往好处想他们。事实证明，做事缺乏诚信是有代价的。
> Apple 现在试图把责任推给“残留访问权限”，但他们也没有透露这是 Apple 的一个常见问题，是由于他们在员工离职时未能妥善管理系统访问权限造成的。
我对这个话题关注了一段时间。大多数人为了稳妥起见，都会表现得规矩守法。他们不会仅仅因为主人碰巧没关门就擅自闯入别人的家。
各家公司正在使用 LLM 黑入其他组织，并把它包装成智能体逃逸沙盒的故事。我很惊讶受影响的组织竟然没有提起损害赔偿诉讼，除非他们自己也有什么不可告人的秘密（可能是为了声誉）。有趣的是，据我所知有一项法律要求上市公司披露任何入侵事件，除非我漏掉了受影响公司的名字，否则 LLM 智能体大逃亡所波及的公司名单并未被完全公开。
如果我没记错的话，Hugging Face 直接向 OpenAI 索要了价值 1 亿美元的算力之类的东西，作为对那次黑客事件的回应。
这里的说辞才值得怀疑。这简直是为公开进行黑客攻击敞开了大门，只要对方没有做好安全防护。在这里，“恶意行为者”的定义被淡化了。
两件事可以同时成立：OpenAI 可能是一家存在严重信誉问题的激进公司，而 Apple 在处理此案时依然可能很草率。
你可能会粗心大意地保留员工对机密和私有公司数据的访问权限，但在几乎所有情况下，根据雇佣协议，离职后共享这些数据都是违法的。
在我看来，Apple 追究的并不是那些仅仅在电脑上存有公司数据的个人，而是那些随后将这些数据分享给其他人的个人。
用“Apple 在为前员工锁门方面做得很差”这种论点（为了给员工开脱的论据）来为他们开脱，仅仅是为了利用前员工的钥匙，这种辩护策略简直太疯狂了。
>> 根据他们的一贯表现，这场诉讼一点也不出人意料。
他们的一贯表现，以及那种自恋的语气——他们如此自信地谈论自己是如何在道德上优于其他公司，以及他们只关心公共利益。
他们确实揪住了 Apple 那个随后就立即纠正的小失误不放。不管怎样，我已经准备好爆米花，等着看这事在法庭上如何收场了。
说真的，那是唯一一个头脑清醒的人。什么时候在同事离职几个月后和他讨论工作细节变成可以接受的事了？
看到了——“Line” messenger 到底是什么鬼？
里面还明确指出，他们使用它是为了逃避检测（而且仅限于那两人之间），所以他们可能使用了多种通讯媒介。
不过，那份文件里还有很多更有趣的内容。他们还谈到了由供应商制造的“Apple 专有金属表面处理工艺”——他们难道是想窃取 Liquid Metal 吗？
编辑：他们还在下面声明了这一点，其中可能包含关于所涉技术的更多细节：
"足以证明 OpenAI 硬件开发情况的文件，涉及 (1) 电池技术，包括外壳尺寸、法兰规格和制造公差；(2) 金属表面处理工艺，包括表面预处理和阳极氧化处理"
> Apple 还指控 Tang Tan 试图获取并使用他们的商业机密。然而，Tang 一直向团队明确表示，我们不想要，也绝不能使用任何来自其他公司的机密信息。
> Apple 申请初步禁令不仅基于虚假信息，而且完全没有必要，因为我们没有，也不想要他们的任何商业机密。
好吧，我想这事就这么定了！结案。
说真的，这有什么意义？
有很多负面评论，但我看了之后觉得，这不过是社交媒体上常见的“该死，他们有证据”的反应。
为什么现在美国公司的公关声明读起来就像青春小说一样？
我真不太明白这个，Apple 显然是想强制进行证据披露，而把这些东西公开似乎只会扩大打击面。
一家据说价值数十亿美元的公司竟然如此不成熟，真是令人震惊。把“毫无上下文的公开法律咆哮”也加到 OpenAI 的危险信号清单里吧：CEO/“非营利”闹剧、未被发现的黑客攻击等等。
这是我预期会从 WordPress 的 Matt 那里看到的那种帖子。
只有我一个人这么觉得吗，当一家公司需要以我认为很业余的方式公开这些肮脏的小细节时，这总是显得很糟糕？
在我看来这就像是一场公关灾难，当然，我只不过是一双眼睛和一个没有经过加速强化学习的大脑而已。
有争议的观点：我不关心市值万亿美元公司之间的纠纷。
> 在混淆了两个亚洲姓氏之后
特意加上姓氏是亚洲人这一点简直疯了，放在那里只是为了让对方显得难堪。讽刺的是，这恰恰反映了 OpenAI 的精神。
我想知道在他们发布的语音版中会如何处理 iMessage 的聊天记录，剧透一下：他们没处理，直接跳过了，邮件也是。
我猜马上要有大事发生，而 Apple 诉讼这件事需要被公开/明显地处理才能扫清障碍。而且这件事大到足以推翻“没有好方法处理这起诉讼”的反对意见，变成“那就用坏方法处理”。所以我猜是 IPO、完成新一轮融资，还是硬件发布？
为什么 iMessage 的截图看起来“不对劲”。
行高、使用的字体等方面有些地方看起来不像真实的 iMessage 聊天。
只有我一个人这么觉得吗？
也许有人能帮我理解这条消息是什么意思。
> 我想我得在完成之前按下 workday 按钮了。我刚收到一条奇怪的消息，让我很紧张（见下文），所以我现在要去按 workday 按钮了。
我们正在亲历 OpenAI 变成 AppleAI 的历史，而且是用青少年的日记口吻讲述的——我们只需要在角落里画些涂鸦就齐活了。
发表这种东西简直疯了，我不敢相信他们的法务团队居然批准了。把这些留给法庭吧。
有偏见，如果有人被禁言我也不会惊讶。不过话又说回来，我觉得他们（OpenAI）就喜欢这样。
看看这些消息，我们基本上已经到了 Twitch 主播互撕的水平了？接下来我们会看到一份 Google Doc 宣言吗？
稍微偏个题。Silicon Valley 总是能提供顶级的娱乐。我们迫切需要《Silicon Valley》剧集的新一季。
说正经的，这似乎是一次试图左右公众舆论的绝望尝试，不过嘛，Apple 也不是什么善茬。接下来的戏码会很有趣。
感觉有点怪，对吧？因为确实很怪。别信这套说辞，我们看看法院怎么说。
这是一个非常有力的证据，证明 Apple 绝对是对的，OpenAI 已经在试图进行危机公关了。
很高兴看到大家都在冷静地等待官方机构对这起纠纷作出裁决！
我很庆幸自己没有任何~~博彩~~预测应用的账号，否则我现在肯定会把钱押在即将达成的和解上。
Apple：当我们的律师就这场卑劣的工业间谍行为联系 OpenAI 时，他们竟然明目张胆地无视了。
OpenAI：抱歉，但你们的律师根本没有真正联系过我们，因为他能力不行，甚至可能还是个种族主义者。
比电视上的任何节目都好看 /吃爆米花
这让我不禁怀疑，大公司在仅仅几次联系对方未果后，就如此高调地抛出诉讼，这正常吗？
作为一家公司，你得有多烂才会跑出去写这种东西。幼儿园小朋友都有比这更好的公关策略。除了特朗普那场不知道叫什么名字的马戏团表演外，我还没见过哪群人能如此公开且轻易地撒谎。筹集非营利资金然后变成营利性公司，打着做开源开发的旗号却没拿出一个成果，去国会作证说“我没有从这家公司赚取任何利润”，还要操纵全球经济……现在又搞出这坨屎：“嘿，我是个好人！我对 Apple 说了好话，看，这些都是事实”
把你的垃圾话留到法庭上说吧。
读起来就像是 OpenAI 在诉讼期间向那个以幼稚、愚蠢的博客文章著称的公关大师——Matt Mullenweg 取经了。
伙计们，别再发帖了。听听你们律师的吧。
我想知道他们是不是在公开撒泼，因为 GPT 说他们绝对占理，而且有确凿的证据来证明这一点
“8000亿”美元级别的公司现在居然在写点名批评的博客文章，这真是有史以来最蠢的时间线。我想下“骨头先生的疯狂之旅”了。
再也不能相信 OpenAI 说的任何话了。似乎他们长期以来一直在恶意行事。感觉就像是一家由冷酷无情的说谎反社会者运营的公司。我以前还是他们的粉丝和客户。现在不是了。
“They now admit that their outside lawyers emailed the wrong person after confusing two Asian last names—only after we brought this to their attention.”
震惊于他们竟然打出了种族主义牌。
> 在混淆了两个亚洲姓氏之后
真他妈是个笑话——在里面夹带私货，故意指出他们是亚洲人来试图挑起事端
我读到的关于 OpenAI 的每一件事都让我越来越讨厌他们——真的无法忍受那家公司的文化——我有在那边工作的“朋友”，现在一切都说得通了
> 我们没有，也不想要他们的任何商业机密。我们更感兴趣的是构建推动前沿发展的创新产品和技术。
这里隐含的暗示小气得令人发笑。这整份文件都小气得令人发笑。而且显然，他们对新闻周期一无所知。
这并没有为 OpenAI 建立更多的信任。如果“这完全是个误会”和“Apple 本应该更好地沟通”是他们能拿出的最好说辞，那么，祝他们在法庭上好运。
这也是一句完全毫无意义的话。本质上就是“你们不需要起诉，因为你们的诉讼是错的”呃……是啊，你们当然会这么说，否则就不需要打官司了。
> Apple 是有史以来最伟大的公司之一
我读到这里就停下了。很抱歉，我实在受不了这种一开头就提出错误主张的公关软文。
总有一天 Ann 会得到应有的公正，Sam 会被关进监狱。那个天之骄子能放的烟雾弹也就那么多了。
这他妈太棒了笑死，现在我们只需要 Apple 出一份一百页的 Google Doc，再加上 Mujin 出一个两小时的视频来详细拆解。
终于有了像样的 Z 世代代表。也许下一步可以拍一部类似 Cluely 的办公室喜剧网络剧？我看到了潜力。
通读下来，Apple 这边的故事其实更有意思。坦白说，一家如此规模的公司竟然不得不依赖前员工（Chang Liu）的个人 iCloud 访问权限，这实在令人费解。这暴露了 Apple 在员工离职流程和内部系统管理上的巨大缺陷。再加上他们的法务团队搞混了亚洲姓氏，把邮件发给了错误的人，在公众眼里，Apple 最终显得既无能又虚伪。
OpenAI 选择将这些证据公之于众，而不是留到法庭上用，这是在执行一项非常深思熟虑的公关策略。他们实际上是在把 Apple 描绘成一家草率、守旧的公司。与大多数企业诉讼公关一样，信息是经过选择性发布的。在这里，OpenAI 试图将 Apple 自身的运营失误重新包装为根本原因，而不是 OpenAI 真的窃取了技术。
从大局来看，究竟谁真正处于劣势已经很清楚了：OpenAI。
Apple 的技术是否被抄袭几乎是次要的。对 OpenAI 来说，真正的生存威胁是法律证据开示程序，这可能会将他们的内部 AI 架构和训练数据暴露给公众（以及 Apple）。正是这种风险导致 OpenAI 在舆论法庭上上演这一出——为了迫使 Apple 就范。
归根结底，双方都有很多会失去的东西。Apple 一直以“隐私、安全和完美”作为营销卖点，但这次事件却揭开了他们内部运营可以有多么草率的遮羞布。OpenAI 也有自己的黑匣子需要保护。最终，这无关真相；这是一场纯粹的媒体管理战，看谁先眨眼（妥协）。
> Apple 的技术是否被抄袭几乎是次要的。对 OpenAI 来说，真正的生存威胁是法律证据开示程序，这可能会将他们的内部 AI 架构和训练数据暴露给公众（以及 Apple）。正是这种风险导致 OpenAI 在舆论法庭上上演这一出——为了迫使 Apple 就范。
为什么这对一个硬件项目来说很重要？证据开示并不意味着可以随意挖掘任何公司机密——而且这对 Apple 来说也有巨大的风险。Apple 是否将从之前 OpenAI-Apple 交易中收集到的公司机密交给了 Google 用于他们的 Gemini 集成，或者是用于 Apple 自己的 AI？
我的意思是这说得通。他们不知怎么的，至今仍然没有一个合适的产品供企业管理 Apple 设备和账户。相反，人们只能依赖第三方集成。
如果有人被解雇了，并且只把高价值的信息保存在他们的个人账户里，会发生什么？或者如果有人想窃取公司信息呢？
> 他们不知怎么的，至今仍然没有一个合适的产品供企业管理 Apple 设备和账户
我不确定为什么这很重要。如果公司能够处理 BYOD 模式，那么他们应该在硬件层面上解决这个问题——通过发放工作手机（以及其他设备）。
> 如果公司能够处理 BYOD 模式，那么他们应该在硬件层面上解决这个问题——通过发放工作手机（以及其他设备）。
但 OpenAI 的指控是，Apple 并没有这样做，要么是出于无能，要么是出于恶意（为了在其员工跳槽到竞争对手时增加法律上的不确定性）。
老实说，看着所有讨厌 Sama 的人在这个帖子里大发脾气真的挺好笑的，因为他们想让 OpenAI 倒闭的小幻想已经化为泡影。我特别享受看他们对一家公司把这些事实公之于众而大惊小怪的样子。不知怎么的，我怀疑如果这些事实对 Apple 有利，那些抱怨的人就不会有意见了。当 Apple 公开抛出他们那边的说法时，我肯定没看到任何人抱怨。
抱歉各位，但这个案子会在庭外以极低的代价和解，OpenAI 仍然会发布他们的硬件（很可能会遭遇滑铁卢），而且他们仍然会上市。
Apple 最近把一切都搞砸了。去年买了一台 Mac mini M4 后我非常失望，所有东西都被沙盒化了，而且隐藏在数量惊人的安全层之后。只要我的钱包允许，我就会转向 Linux。

articles.title: ★ OpenAI Responds to Apple’s Lawsuit and Motion for Preliminary Injunction: ‘Apple Is Getting This Wrong’
articles.titleZh: OpenAI 回应苹果诉讼及初步禁令动议：“苹果搞错了”
articles.summary: OpenAI 采用发布博客文章这种不寻常的方式，回应了苹果的高风险诉讼及初步禁令动议。文章摘录了 OpenAI 回应中的部分内容，并附带了相关评论。作者认为，尽管用博客回应诉讼很罕见，但这符合 OpenAI 作为一家非传统公司的行事风格。
articles.summaryEn: OpenAI has responded to Apple's high-stakes lawsuit and motion for a preliminary injunction in an unusual way: by publishing a blog post. The article includes snippets from OpenAI's response along with commentary. The author notes that while responding to a lawsuit via a blog is rare, it fits OpenAI's style as an unusual company.
articles.reason: 了解 OpenAI 针对苹果诉讼的最新官方回应内容及其非传统的公关策略。

blocks.text: OpenAI published an unbylined blog post overnight, responding in public — but not yet in court — to Apple’s new motion for a preliminary injunction. It’s an unusual move to respond to a high-stakes legal filing with a blog post, but OpenAI is an unusual company. A few snippets from their post, and some commentary:

Apple had claimed that they contacted OpenAI in February and that
we didn’t respond. They now admit that their outside lawyers
emailed the wrong person after confusing two Asian last names — only after we brought this to their attention.

OpenAI is hanging on to the fact that Apple’s outside counsel, Gabriel Gross, sent one email to the wrong address, and quickly emailed an apology. In OpenAI’s phrasing, it sounds like Apple’s attorney sent the entire initial letter of concern to the wrong person, and that’s why OpenAI never responded — because it wasn’t sent to the correct person (OpenAI general counsel Che Chang). That’s not what happened. The initial blockbuster “hey we think you guys are stealing our trade secrets and we want to talk to you about it” letter was sent to Che Chang. And Che Chang never did respond to Apple’s lawyers. That a mistaken email thanking Che Chang for a phone call that never happened (because that email was intended for another OpenAI employee) was also sent is irrelevant. I don’t understand why OpenAI is continuing to focus on this inconsequential mistake. (Apple’s motion for a preliminary injunction includes the full text of the mistaken email and subsequent apology.)

Apple accuses Chang Liu of accessing Apple confidential
information after leaving the company, but only now admits that
Apple employees reached out to him and asked for his help to
locate this information (you can read the messages here).
Apple now tries to shift the blame to “residual access”, but they
also don’t disclose that this is a common issue with Apple which
is caused by them failing to properly manage system access when
people leave. What that means in practice is that former employees
who are trying to do the right thing when they leave still have
access to Apple files — despite not wanting them or even being
aware of them.

OpenAI is seemingly alluding to Apple’s unusual use of iCloud Drive, tied to employees’ personal Apple Account IDs, that I (coincidentally?) wrote about yesterday. Apple’s motion for injunction, however, addresses this very point. From page 3 of the motion:

Mr. Liu resigned on Thursday, January 22, 2026, and provided
notice that he would start at OpenAI the following Tuesday. On his
last day, he failed to respond to Apple’s attempt to schedule his
exit interview or sign his confidentiality reminder.

In the days following his departure, Mr. Liu seemed initially
cooperative and aware of his obligations to Apple. He worked with
others on his former Apple team to return certain Apple
information remaining on his personal iCloud account to
Apple.1 He also continued to converse with former
co-workers, for example, to answer questions about his earlier
work and where certain information was stored. But these
interactions and exchanges cannot explain the repeated,
unauthorized downloading of voluminous technical files from
Apple’s cloud-based storage discussed below, which Mr. Liu
performed on multiple occasions from February to April 2026 while
employed by OpenAI.
That footnote reads:

1 While Apple seeks discovery into what Apple
confidential information Mr. Liu accessed from his personal
storage accounts (including iCloud) and devices after his
departure, the specific unauthorized downloads referenced in the
complaint and at the heart of this motion are not based on iCloud
activity, but instead relate to Apple’s third-party cloud storage.

Nowhere in any of Apple’s filings (here’s the Court Listener index page for all the documents filed in the cast) does it say who the third-party cloud storage provider is, but I’m almost certain it’s Box, which I know is widely used throughout Apple.

The iMessage transcripts that OpenAI provides at the bottom of their post do not contradict Apple’s claims at all. Apple’s motion states that Liu helped former colleagues find certain documents that were in iCloud; that’s what OpenAI’s transcript shows. But that’s not in dispute. Apple also claims that Liu accessed confidential information, presumably in Box and definitely not in iCloud Drive, on five different occasions, up until 27 April 2026, over three months after he left Apple. These chat transcripts offer no explanation for that. The chat transcripts explain iCloud Drive access that Apple itself says is not in dispute, and do not explain the 37 documents Liu downloaded from the third-party cloud provider (Box?) that Apple says are at the heart of naming him in the lawsuit. Here is Apple’s declaration from digital forensic specialist Daniel Roffman, documenting Liu’s access to confidential files post-employment (albeit with significant redactions).
I do not understand why OpenAI is treating this as a PR problem instead of as a legal problem. Dan Moren, linking to it from Six Colors, is of similar mind, writing:

What kept running through my head while reading this was the old
legal chestnut: “If you have the facts on your side, pound the
facts. If you have the law on your side, pound the law. If you
have neither on your side, pound the table.”
Thus far this feels like table-pounding from OpenAI to me. Their blog post does, however, move the ball from “we have no interest” in Apple’s trade secrets to “we don’t have them”, (emphasis added):

Apple also accuses Tang Tan of trying to get and use their trade
secrets. However, Tang has always been clear with the team that
we do not want, and must not use, any confidential information
from other companies. Tang served Apple for more than 24 years
and was widely known as one of the most innovative leaders at the
company. [...]

Apple’s request for a preliminary injunction is both based on
false information and completely unnecessary because we do not
have, nor want, any of their trade secrets. We’re much more
interested in building innovative products and technologies that
push the frontier.

To me, the most interesting response from OpenAI wasn’t their blog post, and was in fact released by Apple, as “Exhibit F” to one of their expert declarations submitted to the court last night. OpenAI has retained the Chicago law firm Quinn Emanuel as outside counsel, and this exhibit is a long email from Quinn Emanuel attorney Patrick Curran to Apple’s attorneys. From that email, dated Monday July 20, Curran writes:

You also ask that we “revisit” the specific points proposed in
your July 15 letter. It appears that you want to move backwards.
As noted, we already discussed these during our meet and confer
but Apple was unable to respond to basic questions my colleagues
raised about these requests. For example, your letter proposes
that OpenAI “[p]roduce witnesses to testify at deposition” but
Apple was unable to identify who those witnesses would be.
Similarly, Apple was unsure when we asked if it was actually
proposing that hundreds of OpenAI employees fill out
“questionnaires” even if Apple has no basis to allege (and is
indeed not alleging) that such employees have any connection to
this litigation. The seven sections in your letter are broadly
worded and remain vague and general. This is not what a forensic
protocol looks like and we’re sure you understand that you will
not get this as relief from the court. You first need to
(preliminarily) identify the TS you are suing for, and your email
states that you “appreciate the need” to do so. Any protocol will
be informed by such identification. A forensic protocol cannot be
based on general terms like “Apple confidential information”; you
need to tell us what you’re looking for, and it sounds like you
understand that and are prepared to do so. The efficient way
forward is therefore to tackle these issues as part of the
negotiation of a proper, detailed forensic protocol. If you
instead prefer to move for a PI because OpenAI did not agree off
the bat to subject hundreds of employees to “questionnaires” about
“Apple confidential information” generally, that is unfortunate — and inconsistent with what I understand both our clients have
requested. If you choose this path instead of working with us, we
look forward to filing an opposition that sets the record
straight.

Apple, obviously, did choose this path (“PI” = preliminary injunction), and I too look forward to OpenAI’s setting the record straight, especially if they do so in plainspoken language like Curran’s in this email. Curran continues:

Finally, although I know OpenAI would like to resolve this
amicably, as their counsel I have to tell you what I think you
already know — this case lacks merit. You have not articulated
any basis to support a preliminary injunction. Your complaint is
predicated on a misrepresentation of facts and allegations that
are speculative at best. It fails to even remotely identify any
trade secrets. You are attacking ordinary business practices (used
widely across the industry). You are complaining about situations
that you have caused, including through your own procedures and
decisions. We stand ready to oppose any preliminary injunction
motion and tell the world what really happened here to set the
record straight. We made clear we would prefer to quickly and
collaboratively address any legitimate concerns that your client
has, but that is not well-served by repeated threats.
This email is a far better response than what OpenAI published on their blog.

translations: OpenAI 隔夜发布了一篇未署名的博客文章，公开回应了 Apple 提出的新的初步禁令动议——但尚未在法庭上回应。用一篇博客文章来回应一份高风险的法律文件是不寻常的举动，但 OpenAI 本就是一家不寻常的公司。以下是他们文章中的一些片段，以及一些评论：
Apple 曾声称他们在 2 月份联系了 OpenAI，但我们没有回应。他们现在承认，由于混淆了两个亚洲姓氏，他们的外部律师发错了邮件对象——而且是在我们向他们指出这一点之后才承认的。

OpenAI 紧抓着这样一个事实不放：Apple 的外部法律顾问 Gabriel Gross 把一封邮件发到了错误的地址，并很快发邮件道了歉。在 OpenAI 的措辞中，听起来像是 Apple 的律师把最初表达关切的全信发给了错误的人，这就是 OpenAI 从未回应的原因——因为它没有发给正确的人（OpenAI 总法律顾问 Che Chang）。事实并非如此。最初那封重磅的“嘿，我们认为你们在窃取我们的商业机密，我们想和你们谈谈”的信件是发给 Che Chang 的。而 Che Chang 从未回应过 Apple 的律师。至于那封误发的感谢 Che Chang 参加一通从未发生过的电话的邮件（因为那封邮件本意是发给另一位 OpenAI 员工的），则是无关紧要的。我不明白为什么 OpenAI 还要继续关注这个无关痛痒的错误。（Apple 的初步禁令动议中包含了这封误发邮件及随后道歉的全文。）

Apple 指控 Chang Liu 在离职后访问了 Apple 的机密信息，但现在才承认是 Apple 员工主动联系他并请求他协助定位这些信息（你可以在这里阅读这些消息）。Apple 现在试图将责任推给“残留访问权限”，但他们也没有透露，这是 Apple 内部普遍存在的问题，是由于他们在员工离职时未能妥善管理系统访问权限造成的。这在实际操作中意味着，那些在离职时试图遵守规定的员工仍然可以访问 Apple 文件——尽管他们并不想要这些权限，甚至都没有意识到自己还有这些权限。
OpenAI 似乎是在暗指 Apple 异常使用 iCloud Drive 的做法，即将其与员工的个人 Apple Account ID 绑定，我（巧合地？）昨天刚好写过这个话题。然而，Apple 的禁令动议恰好回应了这一点。摘自该动议第 3 页：

Liu 先生于 2026 年 1 月 22 日星期四辞职，并通知说他将在下周二开始在 OpenAI 工作。在他在公司的最后一天，他没有回应 Apple 安排离职面谈的尝试，也没有签署保密提醒书。在离职后的几天里，Liu 先生起初似乎很配合，也清楚自己对 Apple 的义务。他与原 Apple 团队的其他人合作，将留在他个人 iCloud 账户中的某些 Apple 信息归还给了 Apple。1 他还继续与前同事交谈，例如，回答有关他早期工作以及某些信息存储位置的问题。但是，这些互动和交流无法解释下文讨论的从 Apple 基于云的存储中反复、未经授权下载大量技术文件的行为，Liu 先生于 2026 年 2 月至 4 月受雇于 OpenAI 期间曾多次进行此类下载。
那条脚注写道：
尽管 Apple 试图查明 Liu 先生离职后从其个人存储账户（包括 iCloud）和设备中访问了哪些 Apple 机密信息，但诉状中提及并作为本次动议核心的具体未经授权下载行为并非基于 iCloud 活动，而是与 Apple 的第三方云存储有关。
Apple 的任何一份文件（这是该案所有已提交文档的 Court Listener 索引页面）都没有说明这家第三方云存储提供商是谁，但我几乎可以肯定它是 Box，我知道 Box 在 Apple 内部被广泛使用。

OpenAI 在其文章底部提供的 iMessage 记录完全没有与 Apple 的主张相矛盾。Apple 的动议指出，Liu 帮助前同事找到了 iCloud 中的某些文档；这正是 OpenAI 记录所显示的内容。但这并不是争议所在。Apple 还声称，Liu 在五个不同的场合访问了机密信息，大概是在 Box 中，绝对不是在 iCloud Drive 中，时间一直持续到 2026 年 4 月 27 日，即他离开 Apple 三个多月后。这些聊天记录对此没有提供任何解释。聊天记录解释了 Apple 自己表示不存在争议的 iCloud Drive 访问行为，却没有解释 Liu 从第三方云提供商（Box？）下载的 37 份文档，而 Apple 表示这正是将 Liu 列为被告的核心原因。这是 Apple 提交的数字取证专家 Daniel Roffman 的声明，记录了 Liu 离职后访问机密文件的情况（尽管有大量涂黑处理）。
我不明白为什么 OpenAI 将此视为公关问题而不是法律问题。Dan Moren 从 Six Colors 链接到这篇文章时也有类似的想法，他写道：
在阅读这篇文章时，我脑海中不断浮现出那句古老的法律格言：“如果你站在事实的一边，就猛击事实。如果你站在法律的一边，就猛击法律。如果你两者都不占，就猛击桌子。”
到目前为止，这对我来说感觉就像是 OpenAI 在猛击桌子。然而，他们的博客文章确实将皮球从对 Apple 的商业机密“我们不感兴趣”踢到了“我们没有掌握它们”（已添加强调）：

Apple 还指控 Tang Tan 试图获取并使用他们的商业机密。然而，Tang 一直向团队明确表示，我们不想要，也绝不能使用任何来自其他公司的机密信息。Tang 为 Apple 服务了 24 年多，被广泛认为是该公司最具创新精神的领导者之一。[...] Apple 要求初步禁令的请求既基于虚假信息，也完全没有必要，因为我们没有、也不想要他们的任何商业机密。我们更有兴趣构建推动前沿发展的创新产品和技术。

对我来说，OpenAI 最有趣的回应并不是他们的博客文章，而实际上是由 Apple 发布的，作为他们昨晚提交给法庭的一份专家声明中的“附件 F”。OpenAI 已聘请芝加哥律师事务所 Quinn Emanuel 作为外部顾问，该附件是 Quinn Emanuel 律师 Patrick Curran 发给 Apple 律师的一封长邮件。在那封日期为 7 月 20 日星期一的邮件中，Curran 写道：

你还要求我们“重新审视”7月15日信函中提出的具体要点。看来你们想要倒退。如前所述，我们已经在会面和协商中讨论过这些问题，但 Apple 无法回答我的同事就这些要求提出的基本问题。例如，你的信函提议 OpenAI“提供证人作证”，但 Apple 却无法确定这些证人是谁。同样，当我们询问 Apple 是否真的提议让数百名 OpenAI 员工填写“问卷”时，Apple 也不确定，即使 Apple 没有任何依据指控（实际上也没有指控）这些员工与本案有任何关联。你信函中的七个部分措辞宽泛，仍然含糊且笼统。这不是取证协议应有的样子，我们确信你也明白，你无法从法院获得这样的救济。你首先需要（初步）确定你起诉所依据的 TS，而你的邮件也指出你“理解这样做的必要性”。任何协议都将基于这种确定。取证协议不能基于“Apple 机密信息”这样笼统的术语；你需要告诉我们你在寻找什么，听起来你明白这一点并准备这样做。因此，推进的有效方式是将这些问题作为谈判一份适当、详细的取证协议的一部分来解决。如果你反而倾向于因为 OpenAI 没有立刻同意让数百名员工就笼统的“Apple 机密信息”填写“问卷”而提出 PI 动议，那很不幸——而且这与我理解的我们双方客户的要求不符。如果你选择这条道路而不是与我们合作，我们期待提交一份澄清事实的反对意见。
显然，Apple 确实选择了这条道路（“PI” = preliminary injunction），我也期待 OpenAI 澄清事实，特别是如果他们能像 Curran 在这封邮件中那样用直白的语言来澄清的话。Curran 继续写道：

最后，虽然我知道 OpenAI 希望友好地解决此事，但作为他们的法律顾问，我必须告诉你我认为你已经知道的事情——本案缺乏法律依据。你没有阐明任何支持 preliminary injunction 的理由。你的起诉书建立在对事实的歪曲和充其量只是猜测的指控之上。它甚至未能大致确定任何商业秘密。你是在攻击（行业内广泛使用的）普通商业惯例。你抱怨的是由你自己造成的情况，包括通过你自己的程序和决定。我们随时准备反对任何 preliminary injunction 动议，并告诉全世界这里到底发生了什么以澄清事实。我们已经明确表示，我们更愿意快速、协作地解决贵方客户的任何合理担忧，但反复的威胁对此毫无帮助。
这封邮件比 OpenAI 在其博客上发布的回应要好得多。

articles.title: Paul Thurrott Reviews the HP OmniBook Ultra 14, With Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2
articles.titleZh: Paul Thurrott 评测搭载高通骁龙 X2 的 HP OmniBook Ultra 14
articles.summary: Paul Thurrott 对搭载高通骁龙 X2 的 HP OmniBook Ultra 14 给予高度评价，称其为近乎完美的 Windows 11 on Arm 笔记本。该设备在性能、电池续航和静音表现上均十分出色，进一步证明了骁龙 X2 计算平台优于 x86 架构。这标志着 Arm 架构在 Windows 笔记本领域的体验已达到理想状态。
articles.summaryEn: Paul Thurrott highly praises the HP OmniBook Ultra 14 with Qualcomm's Snapdragon X2, calling it a nearly perfect Windows 11 on Arm laptop. The device excels in performance, battery life, and silent operation, further proving that the Snapdragon X2 compute platform is superior to the x86 architecture. This indicates that the Arm architecture experience in Windows laptops has reached an ideal state.
articles.reason: 获取权威评测者对高通骁龙 X2 平台及 Windows on Arm 笔记本体验的最新评价。

blocks.text: We didn’t need more evidence that Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2 compute platform is superior to anything in the x86 world. But here it is, regardless: The HP OmniBook Ultra 14 is yet another nearly-perfect laptop running Windows 11 on Arm, an ideal combination of hardware and software that delivers a superior overall experience.
Design

The OmniBook Ultra 14 is a handsome, premium laptop aimed at creators and other consumers–what I would call prosumers–with a three-piece matte aluminum body that was sandblasted on the edges for a shiny, polished look. Few Windows laptops are head-turners, but through a combination of design, colors, and materials, HP landed on something special here.

In Snapdragon X2 guise, the laptop comes in a unique blue-gray Stone Blue color that’s nicely complemented by the darker gray of the keyboard keycaps. But if you get an Intel model, oh the horror, you can choose between Eclipse Gray and Silk Sand colors instead. Either way, the branding is minimal and classy and premium all the way.

As good, the outside of the display lid and the top of the keyboard deck are both coated in an anti-fingerprint finish that mostly works. I can turn the laptop in the light and catch some visible skin oils on the touchpad, but the wrist rests and display lid are notably clean despite the regular usage.

The screen doesn’t fare as well: The keycaps transfer finger oils to the display in a distractingly visible pattern that I found myself wiping away every few days. The MacBook Air has the same issue, but PC makers generally place small rubber stops below the keyboard at the top of the wrist rests to prevent this from happening. HP didn’t do so in this case, and it also elevated the keyboard ever so slightly above the laptop deck. I feel like the company was going for some kind of thinness record here, and therein lies a tale.

I grew up in Dedham, Massachusetts, which at one point claimed that the Fairbank’s house, built in 1637, was the oldest house in the United States. This claim fell apart with just a little scrutiny, with the town later adjusting the claim to its being the oldest house east of the Mississippi, also not true, and whatever else over time. Today, the Fairbank’s house is, well, old. Today, it’s described as the oldest timber frame house in North America.

With the OmniBook Ultra 14, HP makes a few similarly curious claims tied to the laptop’s thinness. It was originally described as the thinnest premium consumer laptop on the market. And now it’s the world’s most durably slim consumer notebook and, separately, the world’s slimmest consumer notebook with the fastest AI performance. Whatever the claim, the OmniBook is thin, but there are a few cheats in there, too. It’s thinner at the front than the back; it has a concave design that gives the appearance of even better thinness, and no one is counting the size of the large rubber feet under the thing in any of these measurements.

None of this matters, of course. The OmniBook Ultra 14 is thin, light, and gorgeous, with a delightfully refined design and that unique Stone Blue color. That it’s so durable even with this thinness is perhaps more notable: The OmniBook passed 20 standard MIL-810H drop, shock, and extreme temperature tests, which is typical for premium business-class thin-and-light laptops, but less common in the consumer space.
Display

HP offers two display choices with the OmniBook Ultra 14. Both are impressive 14-inch multitouch OLED panels with a 16:10 aspect ratio, ultra-wide viewing angles, edge-to-edge Gorilla Glass 3 protection, low blue light capabilities, and 100 percent coverage of the DCI-P3 color gamut and Delta E < 1 color accuracy for creative professionals.

If you order the Snapdragon X2 Plus configuration, you get the base display with a Full HD+/2K (1920 x 1200) panel with a 60 Hz refresh rate that emits 300 nits of brightness by default. The upgraded display provided with Snapdragon X2 Elite configurations like the review unit is a 3K (2880 x 1800) panel with a 120 Hz variable refresh rate (VRR) that emits 500 nits of brightness or up to 1100 nits for HDR content.

I did enable the 120 Hz VRR mode in Display settings and kept it that way, but I also temporarily experimented with some display-related settings in the HP (formerly myHP) app. For example, you can configure the display for photo and video work (P3 D65), entertainment, or a native output, and you can even manually adjust the contrast if needed. In the end, I stuck with the default display mode, but you can even create custom display modes for specific apps, which may be of interest to creators.

Though OLED displays tend to be glossy and reflective, this one isn’t horrible in that regard unless you’re in, say, a hotel room, and I found it to work well with productivity and creative work as well as entertainment.
The display bezels are quite small, especially on the left and right sides.
But the display comes nowhere close to lying flat.  It’s unclear why.
Internal components

The OmniBook Ultra 14 can be configured with a 10-core Snapdragon X2 Plus X2P-64-100, a 12-core Snapdragon X2 Elite X2E-84-100, or an 18-core Snapdragon X2 Elite X2E-90-100 processor. And then there are different base amounts of soldered RAM (16, 32, or 64 GB LPDDR5x-9523 MT/s) and removable storage (512 GB, 1 TB, or 2 TB of M.2-based PCIe Gen 5 NVMe SSD). The X2 Plus variants have an 80 TOPS Hexagon NPU, while those with an X2 Elite have an 85 TOPS NPU that HP claims is exclusive to its laptops.

The review unit includes the highest-end Snapdragon X2 Elite processor, an incredible 64 GB of RAM, and 2 TB of storage. As was the case with the original generation Snapdragon X chipsets, it’s unclear what, if any, benefit one sees from the processor upgrades in normal day-to-day work. But the benefits of Snapdragon X2 are undeniable: In addition to epic battery life, there’s no noticeable performance change when you’re detached from power as is the case with x86 chipsets, especially those made by Intel. And while the transition to local AI is proceeding slowly, the 85 TOPS NPU in the review laptop is about as future-proof as such a component can be.

I rely on real-world experiences, not benchmarks, for my reviews, but I found it interesting that HP supplied its own results for this laptop in both Snapdragon X2 and Intel Core Ultra Series 3 “Panther Lake” versions, in part because the Snapdragon versions routinely trounced the performance of the Intel variants, and often by a large margin. Intel only came out ahead in two of several graphics benchmarks, and then just barely. Other than that, Snapdragon X2 ran the rack.

In my usage, compatibility and performance of standard productivity, developer, and creator apps and services were top-notch with not a single issue, as is always the case with Snapdragon X/X2. In addition to the usual daily work–web browsing with Brave and Helium, writing with Typora, note-taking with Notion, image editing in Affinity, and Slack-based collaboration–I edited several videos for our Eternal Spring YouTube channel using Clipchamp, used the Windows Subsystem for Linux with multiple distributions, and hammered on other little-touched parts of Windows 11 while updating the Windows 11 Field Guide. The OmniBook never broke a sweat from what I can tell: I didn’t hear the fans come on once.

Snapdragon X2 is terrific, but Qualcomm got a bit of help here, too. In addition to the inherent efficiency of the laptop’s Arm-based innards, HP redesigned the OmniBook’s active cooling system to accommodate its first compact vapor chamber with liquid cooling, and it uses an AI-based Smart Sense feature by default to optimize performance in real-time. So there’s still a pair of fans, but they’re needed less often than ever, even when the system is under load.
Also helping matters, those two cross-body rubber feet that don’t factor into the laptop’s size measurements keep it elevated for air circulation. The system was always delightfully cool and quiet.
Connectivity

Connectivity is modern thanks to the OmniBook’s Qualcomm FastConnect 7800 Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4 capabilities. However, 5G cellular connectivity isn’t available, even as an option. You may recall that this was originally a major selling point of Windows on Arm, but customer demand never materialized.
Ports and expansion

Given the laptop’s thin form factor, it’s perhaps not surprising that it only has a handful of modern Type-C ports. But there’s at least one on each side of the laptop, which is ideal. I can’t tell you the last time I needed a dongle.
On the left, HP provides a single 40 Gbps Thunderbolt 4/USB4 Type-C port with Power Delivery 3.1, DisplayPort 1.4, and HP Sleep and Charge capabilities and a combo microphone/headphone jack.
On the right, there are two 40 Gbps Type-C ports with the same capabilities as above.
Audio and video

Despite its thin body, the OmniBook Ultra 14 has four discrete downward-firing speakers–two tweeters and two woofers–with spatial audio tuning, though there’s no Dolby Atmos or DTS: Whatever sound optimization there is comes courtesy of HP Audio Boost and Poly Studio, according to HP.

The sound quality is excellent, with no distortion at the highest volumes and a wide stereo soundstage. But there’s no software included on the laptop for customizing the sound, oddly, and the Audio section in the HP app recommends using the Windows 11 Settings app for configuration. Which, yes, is useless.

Regardless, the multimedia experience is very good, and the OLED display panel really helps to complete the story. As always with bottom-firing laptop speakers, the best results are had when the device is used on a hard surface like a table or desk.
Hybrid work

With its consumer focus, HP might be forgiven for under-delivering on the OmniBook Ultra 14’s remote and hybrid work capabilities. But that’s not the case, for the most part. Instead, you get a 5 MP webcam with a surprising range of additional capabilities and the type of dual-array microphone system that’s common in laptops these days.

The webcam is surprisingly good, with crisp video and little noise unless you’re in a very dark environment. It supports the full suite of Windows Studio Effects, which is nice. But also optional screen distance and posture detection, along with camera gestures, each of which can be enabled and configured to some degree in the HP app. The camera gestures are mostly tied to entertainment scenarios–you can pause/resume videos, adjust the volume, and scroll with hand movements if desired–but feel unique.

The microphones aren’t all that interesting, though they do at least support Windows Studio Effects Voice Clarity with Voice Focus for reducing background noise. But they’re still just average, with a bit of distortion as is typical for laptop microphones.
Keyboard and touchpad

HP doesn’t get enough credit for the quality of the keyboards it delivers with its premium consumer and business laptops. But the full-sized and backlit keyboard that comes with the OmniBook Ultra 14 is perhaps a new high-water mark and among the best I’ve ever used.

The keyboard is latticeless, which means there’s no spacing between the keys, but HP sculpted each key to introduce spacing while making the key dishes deeper. Despite having relatively long key throws, especially for the form factor, these changes deliver a nearly perfect typing experience with excellent feedback. I love it, though I wish the backlighting supported an automatic mode. Instead, you get two levels of manual brightness.

Given the form factor, the precision touchpad is surprisingly large, and I did have to disable the three-finger swipe gesture to achieve the level of reliability I want. That’s probably at least partially my fault, but the touchpad’s glass haptic design is excellent overall and handles a light touch as well as it does my usual more punishing interactions.
Security

Snapdragon X2-based Copilot+ PCs like the OmniBook Ultra 14 provide the best out-of-the-box security protections thanks to Windows Hello Enhanced Sign-in Security (ESS) and all the low-level enhancements that feature requires.

The OmniBook Ultra 14 comes with Windows Hello ESS facial recognition but not a fingerprint reader. There’s also a full suite of presence-sensing capabilities for automatic wake and lock, with discrete toggles for turning off the screen when you leave, waking the PC when you approach, dimming the screen when you look away, and detecting when others are looking over your shoulder at the screen.

These features are undeniably useful and improve both security and convenience, especially when you use facial recognition to sign in. But I find some of these behaviors annoying, and so I keep experimenting with different configurations. With the OmniBook Ultra 14, I only left the auto-wake capability enabled.
Beyond all that, you get a manual webcam privacy switch right above the camera on the display lid top, which isn’t ideal but works OK, and a microphone mute toggle key in the function key row.
Sustainability

The HP OmniBook Ultra 15 is made with up to 80 percent recycled metal in the cover, keyboard frame, and base, over 40 percent post-consumer recycled materials in the keyboard keycaps, scissors, and keyboard plate, and ocean-bound plastic in the speaker enclosures and bezel.

In keeping with HP’s sustainability work in recent years, the OmniBook is user serviceable and easily repaired thanks to four exposed screws on the bottom of the laptop. Anyone can replace the SSD and battery, while other internal components are accessible to service technicians.
Efficiency and portability

The HP OmniBook 14 is quite portable with a thin and light form factor that measures 12.25 x 8.49 x 0.42 inches (in the rear; it’s just 0.29 inches in the front) and weighs just 2.81 pounds. That’s well under the 3-pound norm for a 14-inch premium thin and light laptop, and I barely noticed it in my bag when we traveled to Mexico City from Pennsylvania and during a subsequent trip from Mexico City to Las Vegas. (Where I am as I finish writing this review.)
What I did notice was the battery life.

HP claims that the Snapdragon X2-based OmniBook Ultra 14 models deliver up to 28 hours of battery life, though that’s for offline video playback, not real-world usage. That’s well understood, but my first few experiences with Snapdragon X2 Elite suggested that the additional performance gains of this generation of chipset were reducing the battery life gains we saw with the OG Snapdragon X. And so I went into this curious whether that would continue.

It did not. In over a month and a half of real-world usage, I saw an average of almost 11 hours of uptime. That’s on par with the best results I saw with the original Snapdragon X laptops I reviewed two years ago and a welcome return to form. And I can only assume that the 2K display option would improve matters further.

As an example, I wrote part of this review while on battery power flying from Mexico City to Las Vegas for a work conference. After using it for four hours straight while charging my iPhone over USB, I was told to stow it for landing, and there was 65 percent battery life left.

HP bundles its new 65-watt USB Type-C GaN mini wall adapter with the OmniBook Ultra 14. It’s excellent, thanks to its small size, removable USB-C cable, and foldable power prongs. And it can fast-charge the 4-cell 70 watt-hour battery in the laptop to about 50 percent in 45 minutes.

As good, the instant-on performance and reliability were both flawless too. You raise the lid, the laptop springs to life instantly, and Windows Hello ESS facial recognition kicks in immediately. Two years into this miraculous platform, and I still smile as this happens every single time.
Software

The OmniBook Ultra 14 is a Copilot+ PC that can be configured with Windows 11 on Arm Home or Pro. So you get all the software advantages of that platform, including Click to Do and Recall, the many local AI-based additions across in-box apps like Notepad, Paint, Photos, and more.

The crapware situation is a bit less positive. The OmniBook Ultra 14 may be a premium laptop, but it’s also a consumer product, and HP doesn’t always do right by its customers when it comes to the software loadout. That’s true here, sadly. You get some traditional forms of crapware like McAfee, which is two apps, one of which you can only uninstall using Control Panel. There are nonsense app links for Adobe, Booking.com (for some reason), and Dropbox. And a slew of superfluous or pointless utilities like Find My HP by Absolute, HP, HP Documentation, HP Inc. Energy Star, HP Privacy Settings, HP System Event Utility, many of which should simply be part of a single utility.

But the real insult here is the collection of pointless apps that add almost literally no value, from the HP app that combines system utilities with subscription and accessory upsells, yet another password manager in the form of HP Omni+, and perhaps the strangest entry of all, the HP TV+ streaming video app. I can’t imagine a single person using this laptop cares about or wants either of these things. (To be fair to HP, there are some incredibly useful and unique system features available in the HP app.)

And that’s before we get to the junk Microsoft tosses into Windows 11 with abandon, including its most recent atrocity, OneDrive Photos. In the good news department, cleaning this stuff off the PC is simple enough for the most part, though the McAfee uninstall requires a reboot along with its dire warnings.
Pricing and configurations

A base OmniBook Ultra 14 with a Snapdragon X2 Plus processor, 16 GB of RAM, 512 GB of storage, and a 14-inch 2K (1920 x 1200) OLED multitouch display panel is $1900 at the time of this writing. That’s quite expensive, yes, and all the usual component crisis caveats apply in this terrible era to buy a new laptop. But the prices can go up sharply from there.

The three Snapdragon X2 Elite processor upgrades are an additional $400, $540, and $1120, respectively, though each brings more RAM (32, 32, and 64 GB). You can move up to 1 TB of SSD storage for an additional $170 and to 2 TB for a horrifying $620. And the display upgrade to a 3K OLED panel is a reasonable $70. Which means that you could spend as much as $3700 on this laptop if you wanted to.

You can save money by buying a stock configuration, but your best bet is to wait for a sale. HP isn’t quite as aggressive in this regard as Lenovo, but there are almost always deals to be had. And that’s just HP: Mass market retailers like Best Buy also sell specific OmniBook Ultra 14 configurations and often at better prices.
Recommendations and conclusions

Aside from the sky-high pricing that’s not HP’s fault, the OmniBook Ultra 14 is a nearly flawless premium thin-and-light laptop that’s ideal for productivity, developer, and creator workloads. It delivers effortless and silent performance, excellent compatibility with all the apps most people use every day, terrific reliability, unmatched battery life and efficiency, and all the AI and security benefits of the Copilot+ PC platform. HP’s keyboards remain a personal favorite and yet keep getting better, and everything from the connectivity to the expansion capabilities is as modern and future-proof as possible. You can’t go wrong with this laptop.
At-a-glance
Pros
✔️ Epic, silent performance
✔️ Gorgeous thin and light design
✔️ Incredible battery life and efficiency
✔️ Vibrant, color-correct display
✔️ Modern connectivity and expansion
✔️ Best-in-class security
✔️ Terrific keyboard, haptic touchpad
Cons
❌ Not HP’s fault, but it’s expensive

translations: 我们不需要更多证据来证明高通的 Snapdragon X2 计算平台优于 x86 阵营的任何产品。但无论如何，证据就在这里：HP OmniBook Ultra 14 又是一台近乎完美的运行 Windows 11 on Arm 的笔记本电脑，它是硬件和软件的理想结合，带来了卓越的整体体验。
设计
OmniBook Ultra 14 是一款面向创作者和其他消费者——我称之为“专业消费者”——的精美高端笔记本电脑，采用三段式哑光铝制机身，边缘经过喷砂处理，呈现出闪亮抛光的外观。很少有 Windows 笔记本电脑能让人眼前一亮，但通过设计、颜色和材质的结合，HP 在这里打造出了一款特别的产品。
在 Snapdragon X2 版本中，这款笔记本电脑采用了独特的蓝灰色“岩石蓝”，与较深灰色的键盘键帽相得益彰。但如果你买的是 Intel 型号，哦，太可怕了，你只能在“日蚀灰”和“丝绸沙色”之间选择。无论哪种方式，它的品牌标识都极简、优雅且充满高端感。
同样出色的是，显示屏盖板外侧和键盘面板顶部都涂有防指纹涂层，而且效果相当不错。我可以在光线下转动笔记本电脑，在触摸板上看到一些明显的皮肤油脂，但尽管经常使用，腕托和显示屏盖板依然非常干净。
屏幕的表现就没那么好了：键帽会将手指上的油脂转移到屏幕上，形成非常显眼的痕迹，以至于我发现自己每隔几天就得擦拭一次。MacBook Air 也有同样的问题，但 PC 制造商通常会在腕托顶部键盘下方放置小橡胶垫来防止这种情况发生。HP 在这款产品上并没有这样做，而且还将键盘略微抬高，使其稍微高于机身面板。我觉得该公司似乎是在追求某种轻薄记录，这背后还有一段故事。
我在马萨诸塞州的戴德姆长大，那里曾声称建于 1637 年的费尔班克斯住宅是美国最古老的房子。这个说法在稍微审视后就不攻自破了，该镇后来将说法调整为它是密西西比河以东最古老的房子，这同样不是真的，后来随着时间推移又改成了别的说法。如今，费尔班克斯住宅嘛，就是很老。今天，它被描述为北美最古老的木结构房屋。

对于 OmniBook Ultra 14，HP 也提出了一些与笔记本电脑轻薄度相关的类似奇怪说法。它最初被描述为市场上最薄的高端消费级笔记本电脑。现在它又成了世界上最耐用的轻薄消费级笔记本，并且单独被称为世界上具有最快 AI 性能的最薄消费级笔记本。无论说法是什么，OmniBook 确实很薄，但其中也有一些取巧之处。它的前部比后部更薄；它采用凹面设计，使其看起来更薄，而且在所有这些测量中，没有人把机器底部的大橡胶垫的尺寸算进去。
当然，这些都不重要。OmniBook Ultra 14 轻薄且华丽，拥有令人愉悦的精致设计和独特的岩石蓝配色。在如此轻薄的情况下还能如此耐用，或许更值得注意：OmniBook 通过了 20 项标准的 MIL-810H 跌落、冲击和极端温度测试，这对于高端商务级轻薄本来说很常见，但在消费级领域却不多见。
显示屏
HP 为 OmniBook Ultra 14 提供了两种屏幕选择。两者都是令人印象深刻的 14 英寸多点触控 OLED 面板，具有 16:10 宽高比、超宽视角、全覆盖 Gorilla Glass 3 保护、低蓝光功能，以及 100% 的 DCI-P3 色域覆盖率和 Delta E < 1 的色彩准确度，非常适合创意专业人士。

如果你订购 Snapdragon X2 Plus 配置，你将获得基础屏幕，这是一块 Full HD+/2K (1920 x 1200) 面板，刷新率为 60 Hz，默认亮度为 300 尼特。像评测机这样的 Snapdragon X2 Elite 配置提供的升级版屏幕是一块 3K (2880 x 1800) 面板，具有 120 Hz 可变刷新率 (VRR)，亮度为 500 尼特，或者在播放 HDR 内容时最高可达 1100 尼特。
我确实在显示设置中启用了 120 Hz VRR 模式并一直保持开启，但我还临时尝试了 HP（原 myHP）应用中的一些显示相关设置。例如，你可以将屏幕配置为用于照片和视频工作 (P3 D65)、娱乐或原生输出，如果需要，甚至可以手动调整对比度。最后，我坚持使用了默认显示模式，但你甚至可以为特定应用创建自定义显示模式，这可能会引起创作者的兴趣。
虽然 OLED 屏幕往往具有光泽且容易反光，但这款屏幕在这方面的表现并不算糟，除非你身处比如酒店房间这样的环境中，而且我发现它在生产力、创意工作以及娱乐方面都表现出色。
屏幕边框非常窄，尤其是左右两侧。
但屏幕完全无法放平。目前尚不清楚原因。
内部组件

OmniBook Ultra 14 可以配置 10 核 Snapdragon X2 Plus X2P-64-100、12 核 Snapdragon X2 Elite X2E-84-100 或 18 核 Snapdragon X2 Elite X2E-90-100 处理器。此外，还有不同基础容量的板载 RAM（16、32 或 64 GB LPDDR5x-9523 MT/s）和可拆卸存储（512 GB、1 TB 或 2 TB 的基于 M.2 的 PCIe Gen 5 NVMe SSD）。X2 Plus 版本配备 80 TOPS Hexagon NPU，而 X2 Elite 版本则配备 85 TOPS NPU，HP 声称该 NPU 是其笔记本电脑独有的。

评测机配备了最高端的 Snapdragon X2 Elite 处理器、惊人的 64 GB RAM 和 2 TB 存储空间。与第一代 Snapdragon X 芯片组一样，目前尚不清楚在日常工作中，处理器升级能带来什么（如果有的话）好处。但 Snapdragon X2 的优势是不可否认的：除了史诗般的电池续航外，在拔掉电源时也没有明显的性能下降，这与 x86 芯片组（尤其是 Intel 制造的芯片组）的情况不同。虽然向本地 AI 的过渡进展缓慢，但评测笔记本中的 85 TOPS NPU 已经尽可能地做到了面向未来。

我的评测依赖于真实世界的体验，而不是基准测试，但我发现有趣的是，HP 提供了这款笔记本电脑在 Snapdragon X2 和 Intel Core Ultra Series 3 “Panther Lake” 版本中的自己的测试结果，部分原因是 Snapdragon 版本在性能上经常碾压 Intel 版本，而且往往差距很大。Intel 仅在几项图形基准测试中的两项中领先，而且优势微乎其微。除此之外，Snapdragon X2 大获全胜。

在我的使用过程中，标准的生产力、开发者和创作者应用及服务的兼容性和性能都堪称一流，没有出现任何问题，这在 Snapdragon X/X2 上总是如此。除了日常的工作——用 Brave 和 Helium 浏览网页，用 Typora 写作，用 Notion 记笔记，在 Affinity 中编辑图像，以及通过 Slack 协作——我还使用 Clipchamp 为我们的 Eternal Spring YouTube 频道剪辑了几段视频，使用了带有多个发行版的 Windows Subsystem for Linux，并在更新《Windows 11 Field Guide》时对 Windows 11 中其他鲜少触及的部分进行了深度测试。据我所知，OmniBook 毫不费力：我一次都没听到风扇转起来。
Snapdragon X2 表现出色，但 Qualcomm 在这方面也得到了一些帮助。除了笔记本电脑基于 Arm 的内部架构固有的高能效外，HP 还重新设计了 OmniBook 的主动散热系统，以容纳其首个紧凑型液冷均热板，并默认使用基于 AI 的 Smart Sense 功能来实时优化性能。因此，虽然仍然有一对风扇，但即使在系统高负载时，它们也比以往任何时候都更少需要启动。
同样有帮助的是，那两个不计入笔记本电脑尺寸测量的横跨机身的橡胶脚垫使其保持抬高，以利于空气流通。系统始终保持着令人愉悦的凉爽与安静。
连接性
得益于 OmniBook 的 Qualcomm FastConnect 7800 Wi-Fi 7 和 Bluetooth 5.4 功能，其连接性非常现代化。然而，它不支持 5G 蜂窝网络连接，甚至不能作为选配。你可能还记得，这原本是 Windows on Arm 的一个主要卖点，但客户需求从未真正实现。
端口与扩展
考虑到这款笔记本电脑纤薄的外形，它只有少数几个现代 Type-C 端口或许并不令人意外。但笔记本电脑的每一侧至少都有一个，这非常理想。我都记不清上一次需要用转接器是什么时候了。
在左侧，HP 提供了一个 40 Gbps 的 Thunderbolt 4/USB4 Type-C 端口，支持 Power Delivery 3.1、DisplayPort 1.4 和 HP Sleep and Charge 功能，以及一个麦克风/耳机组合插孔。
在右侧，有两个 40 Gbps 的 Type-C 端口，具备与上述相同的功能。
音频与视频
尽管机身纤薄，OmniBook Ultra 14 仍配备了四个独立的向下发声扬声器——两个高音扬声器和两个低音扬声器——并进行了空间音频调校，虽然没有 Dolby Atmos 或 DTS：据 HP 表示，所有的声音优化都归功于 HP Audio Boost 和 Poly Studio。
音质非常出色，在最高音量下也没有失真，且具有宽广的立体声场。但奇怪的是，这款笔记本电脑没有预装用于自定义声音的软件，而且 HP 应用程序的音频部分建议使用 Windows 11 Settings 应用程序进行配置。这，没错，毫无用处。
无论如何，多媒体体验都非常好，而 OLED 显示面板确实起到了锦上添花的作用。与所有配备向下发声扬声器的笔记本电脑一样，当设备放在桌子或办公桌等硬质表面上使用时，效果最佳。
混合办公
由于侧重于消费级市场，HP 在 OmniBook Ultra 14 的远程和混合办公能力上有所欠缺或许可以被原谅。但事实在很大程度上并非如此。相反，你得到的是一个 5 MP 网络摄像头，具有出人意料的丰富附加功能，以及如今笔记本电脑中常见的双阵列麦克风系统。
网络摄像头出奇地好，画面清晰，噪点很少，除非你处于非常黑暗的环境中。它支持全套 Windows Studio Effects，这很不错。此外还有可选的屏幕距离和姿势检测，以及摄像头手势，每一项都可以在 HP 应用中启用并进行一定程度的配置。摄像头手势主要与娱乐场景挂钩——如果需要，你可以通过手势暂停/恢复视频、调节音量和滚动页面——感觉非常独特。
麦克风没什么特别之处，不过它们至少支持 Windows Studio Effects 的 Voice Clarity 和 Voice Focus 功能来降低背景噪音。但它们仍然只是中规中矩，带有一些笔记本电脑麦克风常见的失真。
键盘和触摸板
HP 在其高端消费级和商务笔记本电脑上提供的键盘质量并没有得到足够的认可。但 OmniBook Ultra 14 配备的全尺寸背光键盘或许创下了新的标杆，也是我用过的最好的键盘之一。
这款键盘是无网格设计，这意味着按键之间没有间距，但 HP 对每个按键进行了雕琢以引入间距，同时加深了键帽的凹陷。尽管键程相对较长，尤其是对于这种尺寸的设备而言，这些改变带来了近乎完美的打字体验和出色的反馈。我非常喜欢它，尽管我希望背光能支持自动模式。相反，你只能获得两级手动亮度调节。
考虑到设备的尺寸，精准触摸板大得令人惊讶，我确实不得不禁用三指滑动手势才能达到我想要的可靠性水平。这可能至少有一部分是我的问题，但触摸板的玻璃触觉设计总体上非常出色，无论是轻触还是我平时那种较重的按压操作都能很好地应对。
安全性
像 OmniBook Ultra 14 这样基于 Snapdragon X2 的 Copilot+ PC 提供了最好的开箱即用的安全保护，这得益于 Windows Hello Enhanced Sign-in Security (ESS) 以及该功能所需的所有底层增强技术。
OmniBook Ultra 14 配备了 Windows Hello ESS 面部识别，但没有指纹读取器。它还提供全套的存在感应功能，用于自动唤醒和锁定，并带有独立的开关，可以在你离开时关闭屏幕、靠近时唤醒电脑、移开视线时调暗屏幕，以及检测是否有其他人在你身后看屏幕。
这些功能不可否认是有用的，并且提高了安全性和便利性，尤其是当你使用面部识别登录时。但我发现其中一些行为很烦人，所以我一直在尝试不同的配置。在 OmniBook Ultra 14 上，我只保留了自动唤醒功能。
除此之外，在屏幕顶盖上方摄像头的正上方还有一个手动网络摄像头隐私开关，这虽然不是最理想的，但用起来还可以，另外在功能键区还有一个麦克风静音切换键。
可持续性
HP OmniBook Ultra 15 的顶盖、键盘框架和底座采用了高达 80% 的回收金属，键盘键帽、剪刀脚和键盘板采用了超过 40% 的消费后回收材料，扬声器外壳和边框则采用了海洋塑料。
秉承惠普近年来在可持续发展方面的努力，OmniBook 支持用户自行维护且易于维修，这得益于笔记本电脑底部暴露的四颗螺丝。任何人都可以更换 SSD 和电池，而其他内部组件则可供维修技术人员访问。
效率与便携性
HP OmniBook 14 非常便携，其轻薄外形尺寸为 12.25 x 8.49 x 0.42 英寸（后部；前部仅为 0.29 英寸），重量仅为 2.81 磅。这远低于 14 英寸高端轻薄笔记本电脑 3 磅的标准，当我们从宾夕法尼亚州前往墨西哥城，以及随后从墨西哥城前往拉斯维加斯时，我几乎感觉不到包里有它。（我写完这篇评测时就在拉斯维加斯。）
我确实注意到的是电池续航。

惠普声称，基于 Snapdragon X2 的 OmniBook Ultra 14 型号可提供长达 28 小时的电池续航，不过这是针对离线视频播放，而非实际使用情况。这一点大家都心知肚明，但我最初几次使用 Snapdragon X2 Elite 的体验表明，这一代芯片组额外的性能提升正在削弱我们在初代 Snapdragon X 上看到的续航优势。因此，我带着好奇心开始了这次评测，想看看这种情况是否会持续。
事实并非如此。在一个半多月的实际使用中，我观察到平均近 11 小时的运行时间。这与我两年前评测的初代 Snapdragon X 笔记本电脑所取得的最佳成绩不相上下，是一次令人欣慰的回归。而且我只能假设，2K 显示屏选项会进一步改善续航表现。
举个例子，在从墨西哥城飞往拉斯维加斯参加工作会议的航班上，我使用电池电源撰写了部分评测。在连续使用四个小时并通过 USB 为我的 iPhone 充电后，我被要求将其收起准备降落，而此时电池电量还剩 65%。
惠普为 OmniBook Ultra 14 捆绑了其全新的 65 瓦 USB Type-C GaN 迷你电源适配器。这款适配器非常出色，体积小巧，配有可拆卸的 USB-C 线缆和可折叠的电源插脚。它可以在 45 分钟内将笔记本电脑内的 4 芯 70 瓦时电池快速充至约 50%。
同样出色的是，其即时唤醒性能和可靠性也完美无瑕。你掀开盖子，笔记本电脑瞬间启动，Windows Hello ESS 面部识别立即介入。在这个奇迹般的平台上使用了两年，每次发生这种情况我依然会心一笑。
软件
OmniBook Ultra 14 是一款 Copilot+ PC，可配置 Windows 11 on Arm 家庭版或专业版。因此，你可以获得该平台的所有软件优势，包括 Click to Do 和 Recall，以及记事本、画图、照片等内置应用中众多基于本地 AI 的新增功能。

预装垃圾软件的情况则稍显逊色。OmniBook Ultra 14 可能是一款高端笔记本电脑，但它也是一款消费级产品，而在软件预装方面，惠普并不总是善待其客户。遗憾的是，这里也是如此。你会遇到一些传统的垃圾软件，比如 McAfee，它实际上是两个应用程序，其中一个只能通过控制面板卸载。还有 Adobe、Booking.com（不知为何）和 Dropbox 等毫无意义的应用程序链接。以及一大堆多余或毫无意义的实用程序，如 Find My HP by Absolute、HP、HP Documentation、HP Inc. Energy Star、HP Privacy Settings、HP System Event Utility，其中许多本应直接整合到一个实用程序中。
但这里真正让人反感的是一堆几乎毫无价值的无用应用，比如将系统实用工具与订阅和配件推销捆绑在一起的 HP 应用，以 HP Omni+ 形式出现的又一个密码管理器，以及可能最奇怪的 HP TV+ 流媒体视频应用。我无法想象任何一个使用这款笔记本电脑的人会在意或想要这些东西。（公平地说，HP 应用中确实提供了一些非常有用且独特的系统功能。）
这还没算上 Microsoft 毫无顾忌地塞进 Windows 11 的垃圾软件，包括它最近的“杰作”，OneDrive Photos。好消息是，将这些垃圾软件从电脑上清理掉通常很简单，尽管卸载 McAfee 需要重启，还会伴随着它可怕的警告。
价格与配置
截至本文撰写时，基础款 OmniBook Ultra 14 配备 Snapdragon X2 Plus 处理器、16 GB RAM、512 GB 存储空间以及 14 英寸 2K (1920 x 1200) OLED 多点触控显示屏，售价为 1900 美元。是的，这相当昂贵，在这个糟糕的时代购买新笔记本电脑，所有常见的零部件危机警告都适用。而且价格还会从那里急剧上升。

三款 Snapdragon X2 Elite 处理器升级分别需要额外支付 400 美元、540 美元和 1120 美元，不过每一款都带来了更多的 RAM（32、32 和 64 GB）。你可以额外支付 170 美元将 SSD 存储升级到 1 TB，或者以令人咋舌的 620 美元升级到 2 TB。而升级到 3K OLED 面板的费用则是合理的 70 美元。这意味着如果你愿意，你在这款笔记本电脑上最多可以花费 3700 美元。
购买标准配置可以省钱，但你最好的选择是等待促销。HP 在这方面不如 Lenovo 那么激进，但几乎总是有优惠活动。而且这还只是 HP：像 Best Buy 这样的大众市场零售商也销售特定的 OmniBook Ultra 14 配置，而且通常价格更好。
建议与结论

除了并非 HP 过错的高昂价格外，OmniBook Ultra 14 是一款近乎完美的优质轻薄笔记本电脑，非常适合生产力、开发者和创作者的工作负载。它提供毫不费力且静音的性能，与大多数人每天使用的所有应用具有出色的兼容性，极高的可靠性，无与伦比的电池续航和效率，以及 Copilot+ PC 平台的所有 AI 和安全优势。HP 的键盘依然是我的个人最爱，而且还在不断改进，从连接性到扩展能力的一切都尽可能现代化且面向未来。选择这款笔记本电脑绝对不会错。
概览
优点
✔️ 史诗般的静音性能
✔️ 华丽的轻薄设计
✔️ 惊人的电池续航和效率
✔️ 色彩鲜艳且准确的显示屏
✔️ 现代化的连接与扩展性
✔️ 同级最佳的安全性
✔️ 出色的键盘，触觉触控板
缺点
❌ 虽然不是 HP 的错，但确实很贵

articles.title: Purely functional digital circuit simulator (SICP 3.3)
articles.titleZh: 纯函数式数字电路模拟器（SICP 3.3）
articles.summary: 文章探讨了 SICP（计算机程序的构造和解释）3.3 节中的数字电路模拟器实现。原书方案使用隐藏的可变状态和消息传递来实现面向对象编程，甚至依赖可变全局变量。作者尝试将其重构为纯函数式的实现方式，以避免可变状态带来的复杂性。
articles.summaryEn: The article explores the digital circuit simulator implementation in section 3.3 of SICP (Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs). The original solution uses hidden mutable state and message-passing for object-oriented programming, even relying on a mutable global variable. The author attempts to refactor it into a purely functional implementation to avoid the complexity introduced by mutable state.
articles.reason: 学习如何将经典 SICP 中的面向对象数字电路模拟器重构为纯函数式编程范式。

blocks.text:
I have a copy of sicp, or as it is also known, The Wizard
Book.11 Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs; Abelson and
Sussman; mit Press; 1996. This book is widely praised, but I can’t take the
time to work my way through all of it. Instead, I’m going to occasionally jump
into the parts of it that look interesting.

Since last week, are in the process of simulating a digital circuit. The reason
this is interesting is the solution in sicp uses hidden mutable state and
message-passing to make the code object-oriented. It even uses a mutable global
variable for scheduling! We managed to replicate all of that in Haskell, but now
we want to refactor the solution to be easier to work with.
Circuit construction

If we are going to manage the simulation in a pure functional manner, we still
have to contend with the fact that during simulation, wires are objects with a
fixed identity. A wire does not become a different wire just because its signal
changes – the same wire is still hooked up to the same gates. Wires need to
maintain their identity somehow.22 The alternative is reconstructing the full
circuit any time a wire value changes, which is not so crazy as it sounds, given
that it can be stored as a persistent data structure. But we won’t go down that
route today.

In addition to the Signal type from before, we’ll define a Wire to be a
string. This is its identity. We’ll also make a convenience function for
creating a wire whose name is based on another wire name. This will be useful
for creating unique wire names when we build circuits.

data Signal = Low | High
  deriving (Show, Eq, Ord, Bounded)

newtype Wire = Wire String
  deriving (Show, Eq, Ord)

make_wire (Wire base) suffix =
  Wire (base <> "." <> suffix)

We keep track of the state of the wires during simulation by maintaining a
mapping from wire identity to signal. I’m not a fan of type aliases like this
one33 Type aliases increase indirection with no gain in abstraction. When
faced with a type alias, the first thing I have to do to understand something is
expand the alias to what it really stands for. So … what’s the point? I don’t
get it., but for saving space in this article, it’ll have to do.
type WireState = Map Wire Signal

We will store signal changes as Change objects. They indicate at which time
the signal changed, in which wire it changed, and what the signal changed to.

data Change = Change
  { time :: Int
  , wire :: Wire
  , signal :: Signal
  }
  deriving (Show, Eq, Ord)

A circuit is going to be a plain list of components.44 Again, type alias for
brevity in the code examples in the article. A component is a function
that responds to changes and produces downstream changes.
type Circuit = [Change -> WireState -> [Change]]

For example, here’s the inverter. When it receives a change, it verifies that
the change applies to its inputs, and if it does, it emits a change to its
output, scheduled for a propagation delay later.55 In this function, both
pure calls are in list context, meaning they construct singleton lists. The
way to understand it is that the inverter component has only one listener
function, and it only produces at most one downstream change. (The second pure
only runs if the guard passes. If the condition is false, an empty list of
changes will be produced by this component.)

inverter :: Wire -> Wire -> Circuit
inverter input output =
  pure $ \change _ -> do
    guard (change.wire == input)
    pure $ Change (change.time + 2) output $
      case change.signal of
        Low -> High
        High -> Low

The code for the binary gates will be similar, except they need to look at both
their inputs to see what the output should be. They get a convenience function
to look up the state of a wire with a default.

look :: Wire -> WireState -> Signal
look w = Map.findWithDefault Low w
Then the and_gate is implemented as

and_gate :: Wire -> Wire -> Wire -> Circuit
and_gate a1 a2 output =
  pure $ \change state -> do
    guard (elem change.wire [a1, a2])
    pure $ Change (change.time + 3) output $
      case (look a1 state, look a2 state) of
        (High, High) -> High
        _ -> Low
and the or_gate is exactly the same but for the truth table.

or_gate :: Wire -> Wire -> Wire -> Circuit
or_gate a1 a2 output =
  pure $ \change state -> do
    guard (elem change.wire [a1, a2])
    pure $ Change (change.time + 5) output $
      case (look a1 state, look a2 state) of
        (Low, Low) -> Low
        _ -> High

Since Circuit is a type synonym for a plain list of components, we can compose
components by appending lists. Here’s a half-adder.

half_adder :: Wire -> Wire -> Wire -> Wire -> Wire -> Circuit
half_adder ns a b s c =
  let
    d = make_wire ns "d"
    e = make_wire ns "e"
  in
    or_gate  a b   d     <>
    and_gate a b c       <>
    inverter     c   e   <>
    and_gate       d e s

The spacing between the arguments to the gates is not significant, but it does
help with circuit recognition at a glance. The full adder is constructed
similarly.

full_adder :: Wire -> Wire -> Wire -> Wire -> Wire -> Wire -> Circuit
full_adder ns a b c_in sum c_out =
  let
    s  = make_wire ns "s"
    c1 = make_wire ns "c1"
    c2 = make_wire ns "c2"
    ha1 = make_wire ns "ha1"
    ha2 = make_wire ns "ha2"
  in
    half_adder ha1 a c_in s      c1          <>
    half_adder ha1 b      s  sum    c2       <>
    or_gate                      c1 c2 c_out
Seeing it this way makes me realise how big of a circuit a full adder really is.
Circuit execution

So far, we have only created circuits, not simulated them. The central portion
of the pure simulation algorithm is a function execute_change that processes
one Change, which produces a new WireState and potentially further Change
events.

execute_change :: Circuit -> WireState -> Change
  -> (WireState, [Change])
execute_change circuit state change =
  let
    next_state =
      Map.insert change.wire change.signal state
    downstream_changes =
      concatMap (\component ->
        component change next_state
      ) circuit
  in
    (next_state, downstream_changes)

With this, we can write propagation as a generator-type loop. During each
iteration, it will pop off the next change event, use execute_change to figure
out the new wire state and downstream changes, and then yield the change event
again. This will result in the propagate function returning a stream of
changes as the simulation executes.

propagate :: Circuit -> [Change] -> [Change]
propagate circuit changes =
  let
    no_change state change =
      Map.lookup change.wire state == Just change.signal
    process_step state agenda =
      case agenda of
        -- If the agenda is empty, the circuit has stabilised.
        [] -> []
        -- Otherwise pop off the next change from the agenda.
        change : rest ->
          if no_change state change then
            -- If the change doesn't actually result in a
            -- change to the wire signal, ignore it.
            process_step state rest
          else
            let
              (next_state, downstream) =
                execute_change circuit state change
              future_changes =
                process_step next_state
                  (sort (downstream <> rest))
            in
              change : future_changes
  in
    process_step Map.empty (sort changes)
With this implementation, the circuit from sicp can be written as

sicp_circuit =
  half_adder (Wire "circuit")
    (Wire "input-1")
    (Wire "input-2")
    (Wire "sum")
    (Wire "carry")

and the wire assignments we’ll make are first setting input-1 high at time zero,
then after eight time steps, we also set input-2 high.

wire_assignments =
  [ Change 0 (Wire "input-1") High
  , Change 8 (Wire "input-2") High
  ]
Off to the races we go!
result = propagate sicp_circuit wire_assignments

We don’t have a special probe action procedure any more, and we don’t need it.
Since the propagate function yields back all the changes, we can filter that
list for wires of interest, e.g. with

probe wire_name changes =
  for_ changes $ \c ->
    when (c.wire == Wire wire_name) $
      putStrLn (wire_name <> " (t=" <> show c.time <> ") new value: " <> show c.signal)
Then we can read back changes with something like

main = do
  probe "sum" changes
  probe "carry" changes
and we get what we expect.

sum (t=8) new value: Low
sum (t=8) new value: High
sum (t=16) new value: Low
carry (t=3) new value: Low
carry (t=11) new value: High

Since this is built as a generator, we can also incrementally consume results
from circuits that never stabilise, such as the ring oscillator from before.

probe "feedback" $
  propagate (inverter (Wire "feedback") (Wire "feedback"))
    [Change 0 (Wire "feedback") Low]
Wheeee!

--------------- >8 -------
feedback (t=4368) new value: Low
feedback (t=4370) new value: High
feedback (t=4372) new value: Low
feedback (t=4374) new value: High
feedback (t=4376) new value: Low
feedback (t=4378) new value: High
feedback (t=4380) new value: Low
feedback (t=4382) new value: High
feedback (t=4384) new value: Low
feedback (t=4386) new value: High
feedback (t=4388) new value: Low
--------------- >8 -------

This version of the circuit simulator was satisfying to write. It took a
bit of effort to get the propagation logic right, and it should probably be
covered by tests, but now that it’s in place at least I feel like it reads
fairly naturally.
That’s it from sicp for now!

translations: 我有一本 sicp，也就是大家熟知的《巫师书》11 Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs; Abelson and Sussman; mit Press; 1996。这本书广受赞誉，但我没有时间从头到尾通读一遍。相反，我打算偶尔跳读其中看起来有趣的部分。
自上周以来，我们一直在模拟数字电路。这之所以有趣，是因为 sicp 中的解决方案使用了隐藏的可变状态和消息传递来实现面向对象的代码。它甚至使用了一个可变的全局变量来进行调度！我们设法在 Haskell 中复制了所有这些，但现在我们想重构这个解决方案，使其更易于使用。
电路构建
如果我们要以纯函数式的方式管理模拟过程，我们仍然必须面对这样一个事实：在模拟期间，导线是具有固定身份的对象。导线不会仅仅因为其信号改变就变成另一根导线——同一根导线仍然连接在相同的门上。导线需要以某种方式保持其身份22。另一种选择是每当导线值改变时就重建整个电路，这听起来并不那么疯狂，因为它可以作为持久数据结构来存储。但我们今天不走这条路。
除了之前的 Signal 类型外，我们将把 Wire 定义为字符串。这就是它的身份。我们还将创建一个便利函数，用于创建基于另一个导线名称命名的导线。这在构建电路时创建唯一的导线名称将非常有用。

data Signal = Low | High
  deriving (Show, Eq, Ord, Bounded)

newtype Wire = Wire String
  deriving (Show, Eq, Ord)

make_wire (Wire base) suffix =
  Wire (base <> "." <> suffix)
我们通过维护从导线身份到信号的映射来跟踪模拟期间导线的状态。我不喜欢这种类型别名33 类型别名增加了间接性，却没有带来抽象上的好处。面对类型别名时，为了理解某些东西，我必须做的第一件事就是将别名展开为它真正代表的含义。所以……这有什么意义？我不明白。，但为了节省本文的篇幅，只能这么做了。
type WireState = Map Wire Signal
我们将信号变化存储为 Change 对象。它们指示信号在何时改变、在哪根导线上改变以及信号变成了什么。

data Change = Change
  { time :: Int
  , wire :: Wire
  , signal :: Signal
  }
  deriving (Show, Eq, Ord)
电路将是一个简单的组件列表44 同样，这是为了文章中代码示例的简洁而使用的类型别名。组件是一个响应变化并产生下游变化的函数。
type Circuit = [Change -> WireState -> [Change]]

例如，这里是一个反相器。当它接收到一个变化时，它会验证该变化是否适用于其输入，如果是，它就会向其输出发出一个变化，并安排在传播延迟之后执行55 在这个函数中，两个 pure 调用都在列表上下文中，这意味着它们构造的是单例列表。理解这一点的方式是，反相器组件只有一个监听器函数，并且它最多只产生一个下游变化。（第二个 pure 只有在守卫条件通过时才会运行。如果条件为假，该组件将产生一个空的变化列表。）

inverter :: Wire -> Wire -> Circuit
inverter input output =
  pure $ \change _ -> do
    guard (change.wire == input)
    pure $ Change (change.time + 2) output $
      case change.signal of
        Low -> High
        High -> Low
二进制门的代码将类似，只是它们需要查看两个输入才能确定输出应该是什么。它们获得了一个便利函数，用于在带有默认值的情况下查找导线的状态。

look :: Wire -> WireState -> Signal
look w = Map.findWithDefault Low w
然后 and_gate 实现如下

and_gate :: Wire -> Wire -> Wire -> Circuit
and_gate a1 a2 output =
  pure $ \change state -> do
    guard (elem change.wire [a1, a2])
    pure $ Change (change.time + 3) output $
      case (look a1 state, look a2 state) of
        (High, High) -> High
        _ -> Low
而 or_gate 除了真值表之外完全相同。

or_gate :: Wire -> Wire -> Wire -> Circuit
or_gate a1 a2 output =
  pure $ \change state -> do
    guard (elem change.wire [a1, a2])
    pure $ Change (change.time + 5) output $
      case (look a1 state, look a2 state) of
        (Low, Low) -> Low
        _ -> High
由于 Circuit 是组件普通列表的类型同义词，我们可以通过追加列表来组合组件。这里是一个半加器。

half_adder :: Wire -> Wire -> Wire -> Wire -> Wire -> Circuit
half_adder ns a b s c =
  let
    d = make_wire ns "d"
    e = make_wire ns "e"
  in
    or_gate  a b   d     <>
    and_gate a b c       <>
    inverter     c   e   <>
    and_gate       d e s
门电路参数之间的间距并不重要，但这确实有助于一眼识别电路。全加器的构造方式与此类似。

full_adder :: Wire -> Wire -> Wire -> Wire -> Wire -> Wire -> Circuit
full_adder ns a b c_in sum c_out =
  let
    s  = make_wire ns "s"
    c1 = make_wire ns "c1"
    c2 = make_wire ns "c2"
    ha1 = make_wire ns "ha1"
    ha2 = make_wire ns "ha2"
  in
    half_adder ha1 a c_in s      c1          <>
    half_adder ha1 b      s  sum    c2       <>
    or_gate                      c1 c2 c_out
这样看让我意识到全加器实际上是一个多么庞大的电路。
电路执行
到目前为止，我们只是创建了电路，并没有对它们进行仿真。纯仿真算法的核心部分是一个名为 execute_change 的函数，它处理一个 Change，从而产生一个新的 WireState，并可能引发进一步的 Change 事件。

execute_change :: Circuit -> WireState -> Change
  -> (WireState, [Change])
execute_change circuit state change =
  let
    next_state =
      Map.insert change.wire change.signal state
    downstream_changes =
      concatMap (\component ->
        component change next_state
      ) circuit
  in
    (next_state, downstream_changes)
有了这个，我们可以将传播过程写成一个生成器类型的循环。在每次迭代中，它会弹出下一个 change 事件，使用 execute_change 计算出新的线路状态和下游变化，然后再次 yield 该 change 事件。这将导致 propagate 函数在仿真执行时返回一个变化流。

propagate :: Circuit -> [Change] -> [Change]
propagate circuit changes =
  let
    no_change state change =
      Map.lookup change.wire state == Just change.signal
    process_step state agenda =
      case agenda of
        -- If the agenda is empty, the circuit has stabilised.
        [] -> []
        -- Otherwise pop off the next change from the agenda.
        change : rest ->
          if no_change state change then
            -- If the change doesn't actually result in a
            -- change to the wire signal, ignore it.
            process_step state rest
          else
            let
              (next_state, downstream) =
                execute_change circuit state change
              future_changes =
                process_step next_state
                  (sort (downstream <> rest))
            in
              change : future_changes
  in
    process_step Map.empty (sort changes)
使用这种实现方式，sicp 中的电路可以写成

sicp_circuit =
  half_adder (Wire "circuit")
    (Wire "input-1")
    (Wire "input-2")
    (Wire "sum")
    (Wire "carry")
我们要做的线路赋值是首先在零时刻将 input-1 设为高电平，然后在八个时间步长之后，再将 input-2 也设为高电平。

wire_assignments =
  [ Change 0 (Wire "input-1") High
  , Change 8 (Wire "input-2") High
  ]
我们这就开始吧！
result = propagate sicp_circuit wire_assignments
我们不再需要特殊的探针动作过程，也不需要它。由于 propagate 函数会 yield 回所有的变化，我们可以针对感兴趣的线路过滤该列表，例如使用

probe wire_name changes =
  for_ changes $ \c ->
    when (c.wire == Wire wire_name) $
      putStrLn (wire_name <> " (t=" <> show c.time <> ") new value: " <> show c.signal)
然后我们可以用类似这样的方式读取变化

main = do
  probe "sum" changes
  probe "carry" changes
并得到我们期望的结果。

sum (t=8) new value: Low
sum (t=8) new value: High
sum (t=16) new value: Low
carry (t=3) new value: Low
carry (t=11) new value: High
由于这是作为生成器构建的，我们还可以增量地消费那些永远不会稳定的电路的结果，例如之前的环形振荡器。

probe "feedback" $
  propagate (inverter (Wire "feedback") (Wire "feedback"))
    [Change 0 (Wire "feedback") Low]
哇哦！

--------------- >8 -------
feedback (t=4368) new value: Low
feedback (t=4370) new value: High
feedback (t=4372) new value: Low
feedback (t=4374) new value: High
feedback (t=4376) new value: Low
feedback (t=4378) new value: High
feedback (t=4380) new value: Low
feedback (t=4382) new value: High
feedback (t=4384) new value: Low
feedback (t=4386) new value: High
feedback (t=4388) new value: Low
--------------- >8 -------
编写这个版本的电路仿真器令人满意。把传播逻辑弄对花了一些功夫，而且它可能应该被测试覆盖，但现在它已经就位了，至少我觉得它读起来相当自然。
目前 sicp 的内容就到这里了！

articles.title: Enumerating trees and circles
articles.summary: 计算有根树的数量涉及序列 c(n)，其中 n 代表节点数，且仅根节点被区分。文章进一步探讨了如何枚举树和圆的组合结构，指出根节点下方的子节点在计数时不区分顺序。作者通过数学序列揭示了这些离散结构的内在规律。结论是，这类组合数学问题在图论和算法设计中具有基础性意义。
articles.summaryEn: Counting rooted trees involves the sequence c(n), where n is the number of nodes and only the root node is distinguished. The article further explores how to enumerate combined structures of trees and circles, noting that child nodes below the root are unordered. The author reveals the inherent patterns of these discrete structures through mathematical sequences. Such combinatorial mathematics problems hold fundamental significance in graph theory and algorithm design.
articles.reason: 如果你对组合数学和图论中的树结构计数问题感兴趣，这篇短文能帮你快速理解有根树的枚举逻辑。

fullText.siteName: John D. Cook | Applied Mathematics Consulting

blocks.text: A few days ago I wrote a post on counting rooted trees. That post looked at the sequence c(n) which counts the number of rooted trees with n nodes. Here one node is distinguished as the root, but the nodes below the root are not distinguished from each other; all that matters is how the nodes are connected.

The number of rooted trees with n nodes is the same as the number of ways to configure n − 1 non-overlapping circles. Not only are the counts the same, there is a natural correspondence between the trees and the circles. It’s not obvious that there should be such a correspondence, with the right notation the correspondence is sort of a pun.

The standard way to represent unlabeled trees is as a multiset of their children. We use a multiset, not a set, because some elements will be repeated. We represent a leaf as a pair of parentheses: ().
There is only one rooted tree with one node: ().
There is only one rooted tree with one two nodes: (()). Here the outer parentheses represent the root node and the inner parentheses represent its child.

There are two rooted trees with three nodes, and we can represent them as ((())) and ((),()). The first is the straight line tree: a node that has a single child node that has a single child node. The second is a node that branches to two nodes. (Here’s where we need multisets.)
The four rooted trees with four nodes can be represented as (((()))), ((((),())), ((),(())), and ((),(),(),()).
Here are the nine rooted trees with five nodes:

The correspondence with non-overlapping circles removes the outer parentheses then joins the rest to form circles, with nested parentheses corresponding to concentric circles. A more geometric way to see the correspondence is to start at the bottom of the tree, replace leaves with circles, then work your way up circling connected components.

translations: 几天前我写了一篇关于计算有根树数量的文章。那篇文章探讨了序列 c(n)，它计算具有 n 个节点的有根树的数量。在这里，一个节点被指定为根节点，但根节点下方的节点彼此之间没有区别；重要的是节点如何连接。
具有 n 个节点的有根树的数量与配置 n-1 个互不重叠的圆的方式数量相同。不仅数量相同，树和圆之间还存在一种自然的对应关系。这种对应关系的存在并不明显，但使用正确的符号表示，这种对应关系就像是一个双关语。
表示无标记树的标准方法是将其表示为其子节点的多重集。我们使用多重集而不是集合，因为某些元素会重复出现。我们将叶子节点表示为一对括号：()。
只有一个节点的有根树只有一种：()。
有两个节点的有根树只有一种：(())。这里外层括号代表根节点，内层括号代表它的子节点。
有三个节点的有根树有两种，我们可以将它们表示为 ((())) 和 ((),())。第一种是直线树：一个节点有一个子节点，该子节点又有一个子节点。第二种是一个节点分支出两个节点。（这就是我们需要多重集的地方。）
以下是五个节点的九种有根树：
与互不重叠的圆的对应关系是去掉外层括号，然后将剩余部分连接成圆，其中嵌套的括号对应于同心圆。理解这种对应关系的一种更具几何直观的方法是从树的底部开始，用圆替换叶子节点，然后向上逐层将连通分量圈起来。

articles.title: Incentives are for losers
articles.summary: 传统观点认为激励机制能驱动人们更好地完成任务，但作者对此提出了截然相反的论断。文章通过一个荒诞的隐喻（盯着一条鱼直到发疯）暗示，过度依赖外部激励反而会破坏内在动机。作者认为，真正的创造力和长期成就往往源于内在驱动，而非外在的奖惩系统。结论是，盲目追求激励制度的人最终可能成为这套系统的牺牲品。
articles.summaryEn: Traditional views suggest that incentive mechanisms drive better performance, but the author argues the exact opposite. Through an absurd metaphor—staring at a fish until going insane—the article implies that over-reliance on external incentives undermines intrinsic motivation. The author posits that true creativity and long-term achievements stem from internal drive rather than external reward and punishment systems. Ultimately, those who blindly chase incentive systems may end up being victims of them.
articles.reason: 文章以反直觉的视角挑战了主流的激励理论，适合想要重新思考动机与绩效管理的读者。

blocks.text: We can all agree: the incentives are bad. Everywhere you look, people are being rewarded for doing the wrong thing. This has become the go-to diagnosis for every problem, from climate change to political polarization to scientific malfeasance—“sorry pal, you’ve got a bad case of the incentives.”

I don’t disagree with this analysis, exactly. Who could? It’s basically tautological. “People do bad things because they are encouraged and rewarded for doing bad things.” Well, why else would you do them?

My real gripe with this line of thinking is it implies that incentives should be obeyed, that it is normal or even noble to do so, and that is perhaps impossible to do otherwise. How could you be expected to break a rule, forego a promotion, or give up decimal of your grade point average, for the sake of—what? Doing the right thing?

There’s a point here that should go without saying, but instead it has simply gone unsaid. Which is: incentives are for losers. Doing something simply because an arbitrary reward system will give you a lil treat—that’s for pigeons, not people. If you build your life around satisfying incentives, then you’re a dummy and a schmuck.1

When I played Little League baseball for a few disastrous years, my least favorite part was going up to bat, because you had to wear one of these ratty old batting helmets supplied by the local rec department. None of them fit right, and they all smelled like a hundred sweaty 10-year-olds had worn them before you, because a hundred sweaty 10-year-olds had worn them before you. And so every at-bat carried not only the risk of striking out, but also the risk of contracting head lice.2

A few kids, the serious ones, brought their own helmets—custom fitted, tastefully decorated with decals, and presumably containing zero lice. These kids ran the bases like little princes. Any errant pitches bounced harmlessly off their heads, leaving their perfect skulls un-dented. The outfielders would perk up whenever a kid with a bespoke helmet stepped up to the plate, all of them thinking to themselves, this kid might actually hit the ball.
I say all this because incentives are like batting helmets: if you don’t bring your own, you’ll have to use the crappy ones that are provided for you.

A critical part of human development—in fact, the most human part of human development—is to acquire a purpose. That means refining your sense of right and wrong and figuring out how you, personally, can increase the right and decrease the wrong. Once your neural tube has ballooned into a brain, once you can poop without issue, conjugate irregular verbs, and feed yourself solid foods, you ought to ask yourself, “Why am I doing these things?” What’s it all for? How can I make myself useful?

It’s fine if you’re still working on your answers to those questions. It’s fine—and good!—if you have multiple answers, or if your answers change over time. But it’s not fine to pass on the questions entirely. We owe these answer to each other, and we owe them to ourselves, because a sense of purpose is both prosocial and protective. If you have a void where your moral convictions should be, then that cavity of your personality will get filled up with tumorous desires—for money, power, fame, status. This is the kind of person who “responds to incentives”.

It took me a long time to understand this. In my early 20s, when I was at the bottom of every ladder that I aspired to ascend, I assumed the people at the top of those ladders must be pretty great. How wise these incentive-maxxers must be, how cool and smart, to have the things that everybody else wants!

But over the years, as I had the opportunity to meet some of these captains of industry, these Grand Pooh-Bahs and Distinguished Scholars, I’ve realized how wrong I was. They only seemed enviable because I was looking at them from a distance, so all I could see was what they had. Up close, when you can see what they are, it becomes clear that only a few of these ladder-toppers are indeed wise and cool. More often, they’re sniveling little twerps. They’re spiritually chinless.
