They have no convictions, no passions, no purpose other than ladder-climbing. It’s sad to watch them, these people who have everything except the one thing that actually matters.

Often, these are the people who are most insistent that the incentives ought to be obeyed. They are quick to swear that good grades, cash, prestige, etc. are inherently valuable, or that they are useful proxies for value. The incentive-obsessives feel this way because they have to. Like the government of a failing nation, they must swear that their currency is real, and they must lash out at anyone attempting to participate in an alternative economy, lest the whole fraud come crashing down upon itself.

Without any formal instruction, approximately 100% of humans will learn to speak, and approximately 0% of humans will learn to read. Talking comes easy and early, enabled by ancient mental structures that hoover up words and extract the meaning behind them. These are the original LLMs, and still the best in the known universe. Reading, on the other hand, comes late and laboriously, piggybacking on bits of brain that were never meant to decode squiggles on paper, let alone comprehend Finnegan’s Wake.

So when thinking about any human ability, it’s useful to ask: is this more like speaking, or is it more like reading? Is this an ancient capability that we get for free just by living long enough, or is this a modern skill that you can’t get without working for it?
Developing a value system seems to be a lot more like reading, because research suggests that many people don’t make it very far.

In the early 2000s, the sociologists Christian Smith and Melinda Lundquist Denton asked hundreds of American teenagers about their religious beliefs. What they got in return was a bunch of gobbledygook. Regardless of their supposed faith, few of these teens could say anything specific about the divine. Most of them believed that God is like, this cool dude who floats in the sky and wants everybody to be happy and to get along, and if you ask him nicely he might help you achieve your goals, but otherwise he’s mostly busy floating. Fortunately, this celestial butler is not super specific about what you should and shouldn’t do, and he doesn’t really speak unless spoken to.3

Smith and Denton came up with a name for this thin soup of theology: moralistic therapeutic deism. They only studied teenagers, but they suspect that many people remain moralistic therapeutic deists for their whole lives—after all, the teens probably picked up this loose handful of beliefs from their parents. People will claim on surveys that they belong to a certain religion, or they’ll get riled up about specific bits of dogma. But if you dig into their beliefs at all, you’ll soon hit a gooey core of underbaked religious mishmash.4

I first encountered this research a decade ago, but when I revisited it recently, I realized something remarkable: this appears to be a rare case where sociologists and psychologists have discovered the same phenomenon by approaching it from different directions. It’s like we started excavating on opposite sides of the Earth, and now we’ve finally clanged shovels.

On the psychology side, we called this discovery the illusion of explanatory depth. As I’ve written before, people seem to understand the world exactly as well as they need to, and no better. Everyone knows how to use a toilet, for example, but they mistakenly think they also know how a toilet works.

I think this illusion is inevitable, given the architecture of the mind. According to predictive processing theory, the mind is always trying to guess what’s going to happen next, and it only updates its guesses when its expectations don’t match its experience. If you run that algorithm for a while, you’ll end up with a model of the world that is good enough, even if it’s not particularly good. You don’t notice the errors in your model until you run smack-dab into them, and every time you correct one, you assume that you’ve gotten them all.

From the sociology side, this same phenomenon can show up as something like moralistic therapeutic deism. People’s folk morality and folk religion, just like their folk physics, their folk biology, etc., are exactly as detailed as they need to be. Don’t hit, don’t steal, take turns, say please and thank you—almost everyone achieves this basic level of moral development, because otherwise you’ll end up friendless, if not incarcerated. Similarly, almost everyone acquires some vague notion of an all-seeing, sky-dwelling God through simple osmosis. (After all, He is kind of everywhere, literally and metaphorically.)

But beyond a handful of high-level principles, most folks remain mushy on the particulars. Smith and Denton didn’t perform the whole illusion of explanatory depth protocol with their participants, but I’m willing to bet that everyone feels like they have a coherent system of ethical and religious beliefs right up until you ask them any specific questions.

Our value systems are flimsy for the same reason our scientific reasoning is flimsy: we don’t fix our mental models until something tells us that they’re broken. So unless your pastor is popping quizzes during the sermon and cold-calling people in the pews, and unless you find yourself thrust into various Trolley Problems on a regular basis, there’s nothing that tells you that you need to firm up your moral and theological convictions. Why spend your days wondering about right and wrong, good and evil, sacred and profane, etc. when you don’t have to? You’re just going to get yourself into trouble, or even worse, into a philosophy PhD program.
This could explain why our sense of right and wrong is so easily overwritten by any half-decent system of rewards and punishments: we just don’t have much written there in the first place.
So how does anyone ever develop a value system that’s more than a few bullet points? I think, in short, that they look at a fish and they go insane.

You can summarize most of H.P. Lovecraft’s short stories as “Guy looks at something so messed up that he goes totally bonkers.” “Dagon” was among Lovecraft’s first: it’s about a guy who gets marooned at sea and encounters a really freaky fish, which upsets him so much that he ultimately throws himself out a window.

This is a useful metaphor, because I think at the center of everyone’s psyche is some version of the Big Horrible Fish: some unexamined assumption that, if you fully considered it, would require you to upend a significant portion of your life.

I saw my fish in 2021 in San Fransisco, during the annual meeting of the Society for Personality and Social Psychology.5 Inside the conference hotel were dozens of talks about stereotyping, prejudice, inequality, and so on. That had never struck me as strange until that year, when outside of the hotel, which was in the middle of SF’s Tenderloin district, people were sprawled out on the sidewalk, dying of overdoses. Scholars were scurrying past homeless people to give talks on social justice, which is ironic because “scholars will scurry past homeless people to give talks on social justice” is literally the main finding from one of the most famous psychology studies of all time.6

Something un-clicked for me that day. I had assumed that the answer to every dilemma was “more research”, and that eventually, all of the experiments being presented inside the hotel would solve the problems outside of it. But as I ate canapés in a ballroom mere feet from so much misery, I started to wonder whether any of us were even trying to make progress, or whether we were just publishing papers. I still believe that the barrier between us and a better world is a lack of knowledge; I’m just no longer convinced it’s that knowledge. I don’t think we will cure the human suffering visible on the streets of San Francisco by running another thousand studies on stereotype threat, ego depletion, and growth mindset, no matter what wonders it does for our CVs.

I saw many more fish after that, of species varied and grotesque. That’s why, on the rare occasions that I enter the conference hotel these days, my name badge does not have an academic affiliation on it, but instead simply says “guest”.

When I meet someone of uncommon integrity, someone willing to defy the incentives at any cost, I find they almost always have seen the fish—big, hulking fish, far larger than any I’ve ever encountered. They have undergone some kind of moral reckoning that undid their illusion of philosophical depth and gave them the chance to forge their own values. They’re the kind of person who could go to the gallows with a witticism on their lips, the opposite of a loser.

I used to see a guy like that every day, although he died a long time ago. Near the psychology department, there was a statue of Senator Charles Sumner, who is most famous for being beaten nearly to death by a congressman from the South in 1856. But that bit of historical trivia doesn’t do justice to the story of his life.

Sumner grows up poor in Boston, living amongst the city’s considerable Black population. On a trip to France in the 1830s, he’s astounded to see Black and white students studying together as equals at the University of the Sorbonne. He writes in his diary: “It must be then that the distance between free blacks and whites among us is derived from education, and does not exist in the nature of things.” He later becomes the most outspoken white abolitionist of his generation, taking positions even his friends think are crazy: the complete and immediate freeing of all enslaved people, followed by Black suffrage7 and racially integrated schools.

Then comes the infamous part: a few days after one of Sumner’s most inflammatory speeches, a congressman named Preston Brooks approaches Sumner at his desk on the Senate floor, accuses him of libel, and then to beats him with a cane until it breaks. Sumner, caught by surprise, is tangled up in his desk and cannot escape; he nearly dies. But then he recovers, and when he does, he becomes even more provocative. In 1861, he pushes Lincoln to abolish slavery in the Confederacy, which causes the newspapers in Sumner’s home state of Massachusetts to call him “a candidate for the insane asylum”. (Two years later, Lincoln issues the Emancipation Proclamation.) Sumner writes bills, arguments, and amendments that are often defeated or defanged, only for them to reappear 100 years later in Brown v. Board of Education and the Civil Rights Act of 1964.8
All that to say: I am guessing somewhere on Beacon Hill, at the Sorbonne, and in the puddle of his own blood on the Senate floor, Sumner saw the fish, and he refused to look away.

I understand why so many people are so concerned with incentives. It’s infuriating to watch villains succeed. And look, if we can stop rewarding people for doing the wrong things, we obviously should.

But I don’t know if we can. Goodhart’s Law, Campbell’s Law, and their corollaries state that every incentive is destined to be corrupted eventually, and so far, no one has proven these conjectures wrong. That’s why discussions around incentives often sound to me like we’re talking about a monkey’s paw that will grant our wishes, but only in evil, ironic ways. “The last time we made a wish on the Monkey’s Paw, it backfired horrifically. To rectify this, we have decided to make another wish on the Monkey’s Paw.”

In the eternal game of cat and mouse between the goodhearted people trying to fix the incentives and the Goodhart’d people trying to exploit the incentives, I am rooting for the cats. We should check whether our incentive systems are having their intended effects, and we should revisit and revise them accordingly. But for some reason, the second we start talking in terms of incentives, we also start acting like courage doesn’t exist and can’t exist. Bad incentives have become our generation’s version of “I was just following orders”, an excuse that should be an indictment.

So we should try to get our incentives right, but also—incentives be damned, do the right thing. If we seek an end to our permanent problems, we must cultivate in ourselves the same three things Charles Sumner said we should look for in a leader: “The first is backbone, the second is backbone and the third is backbone.”

translations: 我们都会认同：激励机制很糟糕。放眼望去，人们因为做错事而得到奖励。这已经成为对每个问题的首选诊断，从气候变化到政治两极分化再到学术不端——“抱歉伙计，你患上了严重的‘激励机制病’。”
我并不完全不同意这种分析。谁会不同意呢？这基本上是同义反复。“人们做坏事是因为他们被鼓励和奖励去做坏事。”那么，不然你还能因为什么去做呢？
我对这种思路的真正不满在于，它暗示激励机制应该被服从，这样做是正常的甚至是高尚的，而且也许不可能不这么做。你怎么能被期望为了——什么？做正确的事——去打破规则、放弃晋升，或者牺牲一点你的平均绩点呢？
这里有一个本应不言而喻的观点，但它却一直没被说出来。那就是：激励机制是给失败者准备的。仅仅因为一个武断的奖励系统会给你一点小甜头就去做某事——那是鸽子才干的，不是人。如果你把生活建立在满足激励机制之上，那你就是个傻瓜和笨蛋。1
当我在少年棒球联盟打了几年糟糕透顶的球时，我最不喜欢的环节就是上场击球，因为你必须戴上当地娱乐部门提供的那些破旧击球头盔。没有一个是合适的，而且它们闻起来就像在你之前有一百个汗流浃背的10岁孩子戴过，因为在你之前确实有一百个汗流浃背的10岁孩子戴过。因此，每次上场击球不仅面临三振出局的风险，还面临染上头虱的风险。2
有几个孩子，那些认真的孩子，带着自己的头盔——量身定制，用贴纸装饰得很有品味，而且大概不含任何虱子。这些孩子像小王子一样在垒包间奔跑。任何失控的投球都会无害地从他们头上弹开，让他们完美的头骨免于凹陷。每当一个戴着定制头盔的孩子走上本垒板，外野手们就会精神一振，心里都在想，这孩子可能真的能击中球。
我说这些是因为激励机制就像击球头盔：如果你不自带，你就不得不使用别人提供给你的那些破烂货。
人类发展的一个关键部分——事实上，是人类发展中最具人性的一部分——就是获得目标感。这意味着完善你的是非观，并弄清楚你个人如何能增加正确的事并减少错误的事。一旦你的神经管膨胀成大脑，一旦你能顺畅排便、变位不规则动词、自己吃固体食物，你就应该问自己：“我为什么要做这些事情？”这一切是为了什么？我怎样才能让自己变得有用？
如果你还在寻找这些问题的答案，那没关系。如果你有多个答案，或者你的答案随时间而改变，那也没关系——而且很好！但完全回避这些问题是不行的。我们彼此亏欠这些答案，也亏欠自己，因为目标感既具有亲社会性，又具有保护性。如果你的道德信念所在之处是一片空白，那么你性格中的那个空洞就会被肿瘤般的欲望填满——对金钱、权力、名望、地位的渴望。这就是那种“对激励机制做出反应”的人。
我花了很长时间才明白这一点。在我二十出头的时候，当我处于自己渴望攀登的每一架阶梯的最底层时，我以为那些站在阶梯顶端的人一定非常了不起。这些追求利益最大化的人一定多么睿智、多么酷、多么聪明，才能拥有其他所有人都渴望的东西！

但多年来，随着我有机会结识一些工业巨头、这些大人物和杰出学者，我意识到自己错得有多离谱。他们之所以看起来令人羡慕，只是因为我在远处看着他们，所以我只能看到他们拥有什么。近距离观察时，当你看清他们的本质，就会发现只有少数几个站在阶梯顶端的人确实睿智且酷。更多时候，他们是些爱哭鼻子的可怜虫。他们在精神上软弱无能。除了攀爬阶梯，他们没有信念，没有激情，也没有目标。看着他们令人悲哀，这些人拥有一切，却唯独缺少了真正重要的东西。
通常，这些人最坚持认为必须服从激励机制。他们急于发誓说好成绩、金钱、声望等具有内在价值，或者说是价值的有效替代指标。这些对激励机制着迷的人之所以有这种感觉，是因为他们不得不如此。就像一个衰败国家的政府一样，他们必须发誓自己的货币是真实的，并且必须猛烈抨击任何试图参与替代经济的人，以免整个骗局轰然倒塌。
在没有任何正规指导的情况下，大约100%的人类会学会说话，而大约0%的人类会学会阅读。说话来得轻松且早，这得益于古老的大脑结构，它们能像吸尘器一样吸收词汇并提取其背后的含义。这些是最初的 LLMs，并且仍然是已知宇宙中最好的。另一方面，阅读来得晚且费力，它依附于大脑中那些原本并非用来解码纸上涂鸦的碎片，更不用说理解《芬尼根的守灵夜》了。
因此，在思考任何人类能力时，问这样一个问题是有用的：这更像说话，还是更像阅读？这是一种只要活得足够久就能免费获得的古老能力，还是一种不努力就无法获得的现代技能？
建立价值体系似乎更像阅读，因为研究表明许多人并没有走得太远。

在21世纪初，社会学家 Christian Smith 和 Melinda Lundquist Denton 询问了数百名美国青少年的宗教信仰。他们得到的回报是一堆胡言乱语。无论他们自称信仰什么，这些青少年中很少有人能说出关于神的具体内容。他们中的大多数人认为，上帝就像一个漂浮在天空中的酷家伙，希望每个人都快乐并和睦相处，如果你好好求他，他可能会帮你实现目标，但除此之外他主要忙着漂浮。幸运的是，这位天国管家对你应该做什么和不应该做什么并没有超级具体的要求，而且除非你主动对他说话，否则他并不怎么开口。3
Smith 和 Denton 为这种稀薄的神学汤起了一个名字：道德主义治疗自然神论。他们只研究了青少年，但他们怀疑许多人终其一生都是道德主义治疗自然神论者——毕竟，这些青少年很可能是从父母那里捡来了这把松散的信念。在调查中，人们会声称自己属于某种宗教，或者会对某些特定的教义感到愤怒。但如果你稍微深挖一下他们的信仰，你很快就会碰到一个半生不熟的宗教大杂烩般的黏稠内核。
十年前我第一次接触到这项研究，但最近我重新审视它时，我意识到了一件了不起的事情：这似乎是一个罕见的案例，社会学家和心理学家从不同的方向出发，却发现了同一个现象。就像我们从地球的两端开始挖掘，现在我们的铲子终于碰到了一起，发出当啷一声。
在心理学方面，我们将这一发现称为“解释深度错觉”。正如我之前所写，人们对世界的理解似乎刚好够用，仅此而已。例如，每个人都知道如何使用马桶，但他们错误地以为自己还知道马桶是如何工作的。
考虑到心智的架构，我认为这种错觉是不可避免的。根据预测处理理论，心智总是试图猜测接下来会发生什么，并且只有在预期与经验不符时才会更新其猜测。如果你运行这个算法一段时间，你最终会得到一个“足够好”的世界模型，即使它并不是特别好。直到你一头撞上模型中的错误，你才会注意到它们，而每次你纠正了一个错误，你就会以为自己已经把它们全都纠正了。

在社会学方面，这同一个现象可能表现为类似道德主义治疗自然神论的形式。人们的民间道德和民间宗教，就像他们的民间物理学、民间生物学等一样，细节程度刚好满足他们的需要。不打人、不偷窃、轮流来、说请和谢谢——几乎每个人都达到了这个基本的道德发展水平，因为否则你最终会没有朋友，甚至被关进监狱。同样，几乎每个人都通过简单的耳濡目染获得了一些关于全知全能、居住在天上的上帝的模糊概念。（毕竟，无论从字面上还是隐喻上来说，他似乎无处不在。）
但除了少数几个高层次的原则之外，大多数人对具体细节仍然含糊不清。Smith 和 Denton 并没有对他们的参与者进行完整的“解释深度错觉”测试流程，但我敢打赌，每个人都会觉得自己拥有一套连贯的伦理和宗教信仰体系，直到你问他们任何具体的问题为止。
我们的价值体系之所以脆弱，原因与我们的科学推理之所以脆弱相同：直到有东西告诉我们心智模型坏了，我们才会去修复它们。因此，除非你的牧师在布道时突然进行测验，并在长椅上随机点名提问，除非你发现自己经常被推入各种电车难题中，否则没有什么会告诉你需要坚定你的道德和神学信念。既然没必要，为什么还要把时间花在思考对与错、善与恶、神圣与世俗等问题上呢？你只会给自己惹上麻烦，甚至更糟，惹进一个哲学博士项目里。
这或许可以解释为什么我们的是非观如此轻易地就会被任何还算过得去的奖惩体系所覆盖：因为一开始我们在那里就没写下多少东西。
那么，人们究竟是如何发展出超越寥寥几个要点之外的价值体系的呢？简而言之，我认为，他们看到了一条鱼，然后疯了。
你可以把 H.P. Lovecraft 的大多数短篇小说概括为“一个人看到了极其糟糕的东西，然后彻底疯了”。“Dagon”是 Lovecraft 最早期的作品之一：讲的是一个人被困在海上，遇到了一条极其怪异的鱼，这让他备受打击，最终从窗户跳了出去。
这是一个有用的隐喻，因为我认为每个人内心的深处都有某种版本的“可怕大鱼”：一些未经审视的假设，如果你完全考虑它，就会要求你颠覆生活中的很大一部分。

2021年，在 San Fransisco 举行的 Society for Personality and Social Psychology 年会上，我看到了我的鱼。会议酒店里有几十场关于刻板印象、偏见、不平等等的演讲。在那年之前，我从未觉得这有什么奇怪，但那年，在位于 SF 的 Tenderloin 区中心的酒店外面，人们横七竖八地躺在人行道上，因吸毒过量而奄奄一息。学者们匆匆走过无家可归者去发表关于社会正义的演讲，这很讽刺，因为“学者们会匆匆走过无家可归者去发表关于社会正义的演讲”简直是有史以来最著名的心理学研究之一的主要发现。

那天，我心中的某种齿轮松动了。我曾以为每个困境的答案都是“更多的研究”，并认为最终，酒店内展示的所有实验都会解决酒店外的问题。但是，当我在离这么多苦难仅几英尺之遥的宴会厅里吃着小点心时，我开始怀疑我们中是否还有人真的在努力取得进展，还是我们只是在发表论文。我仍然相信，阻碍我们走向更美好世界的障碍是缺乏知识；我只是不再确信是那种知识。我不认为我们再进行一千项关于刻板印象威胁、自我损耗和成长型思维的研究就能治愈 San Francisco 街头可见的人类苦难，无论这对我们的简历有多大好处。
在那之后，我又看到了许多鱼，种类繁多且怪诞。这就是为什么如今在我偶尔进入会议酒店时，我的名牌上没有学术机构的名称，而是简单地写着“guest”。
当我遇到具有非凡正直品格的人，愿意不惜一切代价违抗利益诱惑的人时，我发现他们几乎都曾看到过那条鱼——巨大、笨重的鱼，比我遇到过的任何一条都要大得多。他们经历过某种道德上的清算，这打破了他们自以为具有哲学深度的幻觉，并给了他们锻造自身价值观的机会。他们是那种能带着一句俏皮话走上绞刑架的人，是失败者的反面。
我过去每天都能看到这样一个家伙，尽管他很久以前就去世了。在心理学系附近，有一座参议员 Charles Sumner 的雕像，他最著名的事迹是在1856年差点被一位南方国会议员打死。但那点历史琐事并不能公正地评价他一生的故事。
萨姆纳在波士顿的贫困中长大，生活在该市庞大的黑人群体中。在19世纪30年代的一次法国之旅中，他惊讶地看到黑人和白人学生在索邦大学平等地一起学习。他在日记中写道：“那么，我们这里自由黑人与白人之间的距离必然是源于教育，而非存在于事物的本质之中。”他后来成为他那一代人中最敢言的白人废奴主义者，采取的立场甚至连他的朋友都觉得疯狂：立即彻底解放所有被奴役的人，随后赋予黑人选举权并实现学校种族融合。

接下来是声名狼藉的部分：在萨姆纳发表了一次最具煽动性的演讲几天后，一位名叫普雷斯顿·布鲁克斯的众议员在参议院大厅萨姆纳的办公桌前走近他，指控他诽谤，然后用拐杖殴打他直到拐杖折断。萨姆纳猝不及防，被卡在办公桌前无法逃脱；他险些丧命。但他后来康复了，而且康复后，他变得更加挑衅。1861年，他敦促林肯废除邦联的奴隶制，这导致萨姆纳家乡马萨诸塞州的报纸称他为“疯人院的候选人”。（两年后，林肯颁布了《解放黑人奴隶宣言》。）萨姆纳撰写的法案、论点和修正案经常被否决或被削弱，但它们在100年后又重新出现在布朗诉托皮卡教育局案和1964年的《民权法案》中。
总而言之：我猜想，无论是在比肯山、索邦大学，还是在参议院大厅他自己的一滩血泊中，萨姆纳都看到了那条鱼，并且拒绝移开视线。
我理解为什么这么多人如此关注激励机制。看着坏人得逞令人气愤。而且听着，如果我们能停止奖励做错事的人，我们显然应该这么做。
但我不知道我们是否能做到。古德哈特定律、坎贝尔定律及其推论指出，每种激励机制最终都注定会被腐蚀，而且到目前为止，还没有人证明这些猜想是错的。这就是为什么围绕激励机制的讨论在我听来，就像我们在谈论一只猴爪，它会实现我们的愿望，但只会以邪恶、讽刺的方式实现。“上次我们向猴爪许愿，结果惨遭反噬。为了纠正这一点，我们决定再次向猴爪许愿。”
在试图修复激励机制的好心人与试图利用激励机制的“古德哈特”人之间永恒的猫鼠游戏中，我支持猫。我们应该检查我们的激励机制是否达到了预期效果，并据此重新审视和修改它们。但出于某种原因，当我们开始用激励机制来谈论问题时，我们也开始表现得好像勇气根本不存在也不可能存在一样。糟糕的激励机制已经成了我们这一代人的“我只是在服从命令”，这本该是一项指控，却成了一个借口。
所以我们应该努力把激励机制弄对，但同时——去他的激励机制，做正确的事。如果我们寻求彻底解决我们长期存在的问题，我们必须在自己身上培养查尔斯·萨姆纳所说的我们应该在领导者身上寻找的那三样东西：“第一是骨气，第二是骨气，第三还是骨气。”
特别感谢 Tal Yarkoni 的这篇文章和 Alice Maz 的这条推文，我很久以前看过它们，毫无疑问它们在精神上启发了这篇文章：
只有傻瓜和懦夫才会“对激励做出反应”。健康的人在切实可行的情况下做自己想做的事，而伟大的人无论遇到什么情况都会做自己想做的事。
大家都知道，如果真的被棒球砸中头部，这些头盔上被咬过、烂掉的泡沫根本起不到什么保护作用。它们的作用更多是仪式性的，而非实用性的，就像厨师的厨师帽或教皇的主教冠一样。
正如史密斯和丹顿研究中的一位参与者，一位来自加州的穆斯林男孩所说的那样：
上帝就像一个实体，决定着何时、是否要干预许多事情。对我来说，上帝基本上就等同于干预，就像极度的运气。比如你买某样东西刚好差50美元，然后你在地上捡到了50美元，那可能就是上帝的干预或类似的事情。但除此之外，他似乎只是在监视。他只是退居幕后看着，就像在看一出戏，就像他是个制片人。他让这出戏成为可能，然后看着它，如果有他不喜欢的地方，他就会去改变它。
调查研究得出了类似的结论。例如，天主教徒和新教徒曾因教义争端而互相残杀了几个世纪。然而今天，只有大约一半的天主教徒知道，与新教徒不同，他们本应相信“变体论”——即弥撒中使用的面包和葡萄酒会变成耶稣真实的身体和血。与此同时，大约一半的新教徒不知道马丁·路德是谁。
这件事发生在二月，就在covid在美国真正爆发之前。我记得我的导师警告我不要去，但我没理会他，还搬出了心理偏见的标准武器库来反驳他：聚焦错觉、范围忽视、可得性启发式。当我向他道歉时，只能通过Zoom来进行。

在20世纪70年代，两位心理学家招募了一批神学院学生来做一次简短的演讲，内容要么是关于神学院毕业生的就业机会，要么是关于好撒马利亚人的故事。其中一些人被告知他们演讲已经迟到了，需要抓紧时间，或者被告知他们准时或提前了。在他们前往发表演讲的大楼的路上，所有参与者都经过了一个瘫倒在门口的男人身边，他在十二月的寒风中呻吟咳嗽。处于“匆忙”条件下的参与者不太可能停下来帮忙；他们演讲的内容并不重要。正如那个时代的许多研究一样，参与者数量不足以确定这些结果是否稳健，但我很乐观地认为，你能够再次发现这样的效应。
至少对男人来说是这样。遗憾的是，萨姆纳从来都不是女性的拥护者。他的传记作者暗示他可能是同性恋，而且他可能对异性抱有某种怨恨。他和一位男性朋友交换过轻佻的信件，当那位朋友结婚时，他感到十分沮丧。萨姆纳自己直到50多岁才结婚，结果他的妻子立刻开始公开出轨，几个月后又抛弃了他。她告诉所有人他阳痿，这给他的政敌提供了无尽的弹药。

articles.title: Committing to creativity
articles.summary: 创造力不仅依赖于瞬间的灵感或动机，更需要长期的承诺与坚持。文章探讨了承诺与动机之间的微妙界限，指出动机往往是短暂且易受情绪影响的，而承诺则是维持持续创作的基石。作者认为，将创意转化为实际成果需要跨越这一界限，建立稳定的创作习惯。结论是，只有通过坚定的承诺，才能在缺乏动机时依然保持创造力。
articles.summaryEn: Creativity relies not just on fleeting inspiration or motivation, but more importantly on long-term commitment and persistence. The article explores the fine line between commitment and motivation, pointing out that motivation is often transient and emotionally driven, whereas commitment is the cornerstone of sustained creation. The author argues that turning ideas into tangible results requires crossing this line and building stable creative habits. Ultimately, only through firm commitment can one maintain creativity even when motivation is lacking.
articles.reason: 深刻剖析了动机与承诺在创作过程中的不同作用，为创作者提供了克服灵感枯竭的实用视角。

blocks.text: There's a quote from the book City of Thieves by David Benioff where a character laments the fickleness of talent:

Talent must be a fanatical mistress. She's beautiful; when you're with her, people watch you, they notice. But she bangs on your door at odd hours, and she disappears for long stretches, and she has no patience for the rest of your existence; your wife, your children, your friends. She is the most thrilling evening of your week, but some day she will leave you for good. One night, after she's been gone for years, you will see her on the arm of a younger man, and she will pretend not to recognize you.
While I love this quote, as well as the book (you should definitely read it), I can't help but disagree with the premise that talent and creativity are divinely bestowed and out of your control.

I've read a few autobiographies of prolific authors, and they all state the same thing: the words don't come easily and sometimes need to be dragged, kicking and screaming, into the light. The book Creativity by the winner of the most-difficult-to-pronounce-name-award, Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, shares this conclusion and suggests that creativity is a creature to be nurtured, given space to grow, and needs commitment and a lack of distractions to thrive.
The thesis is clear: relying on motivation is a losing game. Motivation is a feeling, while commitment is a decision that outlives the feeling.

I've found this to be true in my own life, both in creative pursuits, and in things like relationships and exercise. It is a rare person who is amped to exercise all the time, and so it requires commitment to stick with it. Similarly, showing up well in your relationships can't depend on fleeting passions, because life is bumpy.

The nice thing is that commitments become easier with time. I have near zero resistance to exercising and journalling, and have been doing both almost every day for close to a decade. The first year or two were difficult, but once they were a part of my day, they became absurdly easy to continue doing. Relatedly, when I'm in a good writing routine it is effortless to write. However, if I go a month without writing on my blog (as is currently the case), each word is a struggle.
Action begets motivation, not the other way around.

Creativity is like a muscle. It requires constant use to grow, and atrophies when neglected. But creativity is transferable, and so, engaging creatively has positive effects in other creative domains. This post was inspired by a comic jam I attended this past weekend. The comics were great, genuinely funny, and everyone had a wholesome time. It also made me realise how long it had been since I'd sketched.
Conversely, I speculate that forgoing creative thought will lead to it "leaving you for a younger man". She doesn't leave on a whim, she leaves when you stop showing up.

It hurts when I see people "brainstorming with AI". This is essentially offloading creative thought to a machine, forgoing the most human of processes. It honestly makes me sad, and I can't help but feel that collectively we’re losing something beautiful. The machines are coming for so much, but we can’t let them have this.
So go do something creative. Anything. Make a zine, paint with some watercolours, come up with a song. And keep doing that, forever.

translations: 大卫·贝尼奥夫的著作《贼城》中有一段引文，书中一个角色感叹了才华的善变：
才华必定是个狂热的情妇。她很美丽；当你和她在一起时，人们会注视你，注意到你。但她会在奇怪的时间敲你的门，又会消失很长一段时间，而且她对你生活中的其他部分毫无耐心；你的妻子、你的孩子、你的朋友。她是你一周中最激动人心的夜晚，但总有一天她会永远离开你。某天夜里，在她离开多年之后，你会看到她挽着一个更年轻的男人的手臂，而她会假装不认识你。
虽然我很喜欢这段引文，也很喜欢这本书（你绝对应该读一读），但我忍不住不同意这样一个前提：才华和创造力是上天赐予的，且不受你控制。
我读过几本多产作家的自传，他们都表达了同样的观点：文字来之不易，有时需要连拖带拽、连踢带叫地拖到光天化日之下。名字最难发音奖得主米哈里·契克森米哈赖所著的《创造力》一书也分享了这一结论，并提出创造力是一种需要被培养、给予成长空间的生物，它需要投入和免受干扰才能茁壮成长。
结论很明确：依赖动力是一场必输的游戏。动力是一种感觉，而投入是一种比感觉更长久的决定。
我发现在我自己的生活中也是如此，无论是在创意追求上，还是在人际关系和锻炼等事情上。很少有人能一直对锻炼充满热情，因此需要投入才能坚持下去。同样，在人际关系中表现出色不能依赖于转瞬即逝的激情，因为生活是颠簸的。
好消息是，随着时间的推移，坚持会变得更容易。我对锻炼和写日记几乎没有抵触情绪，并且近十年来几乎每天都在做这两件事。头一两年很困难，但一旦它们成为我日常生活的一部分，继续做下去就变得异常容易。与此相关的是，当我处于良好的写作习惯中时，写作毫不费力。然而，如果我一个月不在博客上写东西（就像现在这样），每个字都是一种挣扎。
行动产生动力，而不是相反。
创造力就像肌肉。它需要不断使用才能生长，被忽视时就会萎缩。但创造力是可以迁移的，因此，参与创意活动会对其他创意领域产生积极影响。这篇文章的灵感来自于我上个周末参加的一场漫画创作聚会。那些漫画很棒，真的很有趣，每个人都度过了愉快的时光。这也让我意识到我已经有多久没有画画了。
相反，我推测放弃创造性思维会导致它“为了一个更年轻的男人离开你”。她不会一时兴起离开，她是在你不再出现时离开的。
当我看到人们“用 AI 头脑风暴”时，我感到心痛。这本质上是将创造性思维外包给机器，放弃了最具有人性的过程。说实话，这让我感到难过，我不禁觉得我们作为一个整体正在失去一些美好的东西。机器正在夺走很多东西，但我们不能让它们夺走这个。
所以，去做点有创意的事吧。什么都行。做一本小众杂志，画些水彩画，创作一首歌。然后永远坚持下去。

articles.title: Gadget Review: T2 Max plug-in Thermal Camera ★★★⯪☆
articles.titleZh: 设备评测：T2 Max 插入式热像仪 ★★★⯪☆
articles.summary: Thermal Master 推出的 T2 Max 是一款专为手机设计的 USB-C 插入式热像仪，体积小巧且重量适中。与上一代带大触摸屏的笨重设备不同，T2 Max 的加长 USB-C 接头使其能够兼容佩戴手机壳的设备。这款相机主打便携性和即插即用，降低了热成像技术的使用门槛。评测者给出了三星半的评价，认为它在便携性与功能性之间取得了良好平衡。
articles.summaryEn: The T2 Max by Thermal Master is a compact and lightweight USB-C plug-in thermal camera designed for smartphones. Unlike its bulky predecessor with a large touchscreen, the T2 Max features an extended USB-C connector that accommodates phones even with cases on. This camera focuses on portability and plug-and-play convenience, lowering the barrier to using thermal imaging technology. The reviewer gave it a 3.5-star rating, noting a good balance between portability and functionality.
articles.reason: 如果你需要一款随身携带、即插即用的热成像设备，这篇评测详细介绍了 T2 Max 的便携设计与实际兼容性表现。

blocks.text: The good folks at Thermal Master have sent me another Thermal Camera to review. The last one was a big beastie with a huge touchscreen. This one is much smaller and is designed to plug into your phone's USB-C port.
The T2 Max is a chunky little camera - but doesn't weight too much. The USB-C connector is long enough to securely plug in even if your phone is wearing a case.
Thermal Master boasts that this is the "world's smallest thermal monocular" - and it is easy to believe. The lens is comparatively huge, but the total package size is tiny.
In the box you get the camera module with rubber lens cover, a short extension lead, a Lightning adapter, and a handy carry case which is well-padded and has a carabiner clip.
The focus is manually adjustable. Gently twist the lens until you can clearly see what it is pointed at.
Wanna see some photos?
Photos
These are the original photos, untouched. Annoyingly, the images are rotated 90°, so I've fixed that. I've also removed the geolocation.
Photos are 1008x1344 pixels. Of course, that's massively upscaled - still, the level of detail is impressive.
Here's a cat I spotted.
Turning on the X3 enhanced mode, and you can see the amount of extra detail it extracts.
There's a variety of thermal modes. Particularly effective is this one which highlights heat in green and lets the rest of the image fade away. Very good for birdwatching.
The zoom is relatively impressive, and the picture-in-picture mode allows you to see an optical image as well as thermal. Here's the moon.
Videos
Video is about 25MB per minute with a resolution of 672x504. Here's a re-encoded video showing off the various thermal modes, focuses, etc.
Your device's microphone can be used to record an audio track. That's useful for giving commentary on what you're seeing. I've stripped it out because you don't need to hear me chatting to the cat.
The camera can pick up a remarkable amount of detail - although the zoom is digital rather than optical.
Framerate starts off well but, as you can see, degrades a bit. I suspect that's the app's fault. It's a real shame because the phone screen seems to display a silky-smooth frame rate.
Android App
Once you've installed the Thermal Master app, you can set it to open as soon as the camera is plugged in.
The app takes a bit of getting used to. There's no direct on-screen "take photo" button, you have to open it up from a menu, which is a little annoying.
There are a decent amount of options to fiddle about with. Because USB-C is bidirectional, the camera can either face you or away from you. If you swap orientation you'll need to adjust the settings.
It also has a "Picture in Picture" mode which overlays the thermal image with what your device's regular camera is seeing. That's handy in daytime, but a bit pointless at night.
Sadly, the app is a bit crap. It crashed several times while I was using it.
The interface isn't brilliant and you'll find yourself taking several taps to do anything basic.
iOS Support
No idea. It should work with newer USB-C iPhones. It also comes with an adapter for older Lightning port devices.
Linux Support
Nope. I tried using the extension cable and plugging it directly into my computer's USB-C ports. I got this series of errors from dmesg:

device descriptor read/64, error -32
attempt power cycle
new full-speed USB device number 17 using xhci_hcd
Device not responding to setup address.
device not accepting address 17, error -71
WARN: invalid context state for evaluate context command.
unable to enumerate USB device

I rotated the cable, and it showed up as 3474:41b2 Thermal Master Technology Co., Ltd. T2 Max. I suspect that it doesn't have the internal resistors needed to signal that it is a USB 2 device - and the included extension cable is wired to only provide them on one orientation. Even after all that, I couldn't get it working in any standard Linux tools.
To be fair, it isn't marketed as being suitable for computer use. It explicitly says iPhone and Android only. Ah well!
Price
Thermal Cameras are expensive - even more so when they're miniaturised like this. So, brace yourself, it is on sale for £320!
Readers can use the code THERMBIRD10 for 10% off at Thermal Master website, or Amazon UK, or Amazon.com.
Final Thoughts
If you spend a lot of time looking for wildlife, The T2 Max is a decent bit of kit. It is small, lightweight, and easy to integrate with your phone.

The app is a real let down. It isn't exactly the zenith of interaction design - but you'll find your way round it easily enough. The real problem is the frequent crashes an the lapses in frame-rate while recording video.
Because of the design of the lens, it isn't great for domestic tasks like spotting leaks & hotspots. For that you'll want something like the Hikmicro unit I reviewed last week.

Being able to shove it into your phone means that it can easily integrate into your workflow. You can edit, crop, and post images just as you normally do. For such a small device, you get a lot of image - and the on-board processing is excellent.
Sadly, the zoom is digital, rather than optical. All you're doing is blowing up pixels rather than getting closer to the subject.
The image quality is exquisite but the Android app is a real let down. If you're prepared to put up with a baffling interface and occasional crashes, you'll get some fine photos and videos out of it.

translations: Thermal Master 的好心人又给我寄了一台热成像仪来评测。上一台是个带巨大触摸屏的大块头。这台要小得多，设计为直接插入手机的 USB-C 接口。
T2 Max 是一台略显厚重的小相机——但重量并不算大。它的 USB-C 接口足够长，即使手机戴着保护壳也能稳固插入。
Thermal Master 吹嘘这是“世界上最小的热成像单筒望远镜”——这很容易让人相信。镜头相对较大，但整体尺寸非常小巧。
包装盒内包含带有橡胶镜头盖的相机模块、一根短延长线、一个 Lightning 转接头，以及一个带有衬垫和登山扣的便携包。
焦距是手动调节的。轻轻转动镜头，直到能清晰地看到对准的物体。
想看几张照片吗？
照片
这些是未经处理的原始照片。令人烦恼的是，图像旋转了 90°，所以我修正了这个问题。我还移除了地理位置信息。
照片分辨率为 1008x1344 像素。当然，这是大幅放大后的结果——尽管如此，细节水平依然令人印象深刻。
这是我看到的一只猫。
开启 X3 增强模式后，你可以看到它提取出的额外细节量。
这里有多种热成像模式。其中特别有效的是这种模式，它用绿色突出热量，并让图像的其余部分淡出。非常适合观鸟。
变焦能力相当不错，画中画模式允许你同时查看光学图像和热成像。这是月亮。
视频
视频大约每分钟 25MB，分辨率为 672x504。这里有一段重新编码的视频，展示了各种热成像模式、对焦等。
可以使用设备的麦克风录制音轨。这对于为你看到的内容进行解说很有用。我已经把音轨去掉了，因为你不需要听我跟猫聊天。
这款相机能捕捉到惊人的细节量——尽管它的变焦是数字变焦而非光学变焦。
帧率一开始很好，但如你所见，后来会有所下降。我怀疑这是应用程序的问题。这真的很遗憾，因为手机屏幕似乎能显示丝般顺滑的帧率。
Android 应用程序
安装好 Thermal Master 应用程序后，你可以将其设置为在插入相机时自动打开。
这个应用程序需要一点时间来适应。屏幕上没有直接的“拍照”按钮，你必须从菜单中打开它，这有点烦人。
有相当多的选项可供调整。由于 USB-C 是双向的，相机可以面向你或背向你。如果改变方向，你需要调整设置。
它还有一个“画中画”模式，可以将热成像图像与设备普通摄像头看到的画面叠加。这在白天很方便，但在晚上就有点没意义了。
遗憾的是，这个应用程序有点糟糕。我在使用它时它崩溃了好几次。
界面并不出色，你会发现做任何基本操作都需要点击好几次。
iOS 支持
不太清楚。它应该能和较新的 USB-C iPhone 一起使用。它还附带了一个用于较旧 Lightning 接口设备的转接头。
Linux 支持
不支持。我尝试使用延长线并将其直接插入电脑的 USB-C 接口。我从 dmesg 收到了以下一系列错误：

device descriptor read/64, error -32
attempt power cycle
new full-speed USB device number 17 using xhci_hcd
Device not responding to setup address.
device not accepting address 17, error -71
WARN: invalid context state for evaluate context command.
unable to enumerate USB device
我翻转了线缆，它显示为 3474:41b2 Thermal Master Technology Co., Ltd. T2 Max。我怀疑它缺少用于标识其为 USB 2 设备的内部电阻——而且附带的延长线在接线时只在一个方向上提供这些电阻。即使折腾了这么多，我还是无法在任何标准 Linux 工具中让它正常工作。
平心而论，它并没有标榜适合在电脑上使用。它明确说明仅支持 iPhone 和 Android。哎，算了吧！
价格
热成像仪价格不菲——像这样微型化之后更是如此。所以，做好心理准备吧，它的售价高达 320 英镑！
读者可以使用代码 THERMBIRD10 在 Thermal Master 官网、Amazon UK 或 Amazon.com 上享受 9 折优惠。
总结
如果你经常花时间寻找野生动物，T2 Max 是一款相当不错的装备。它体积小巧、重量轻，而且很容易与手机配合使用。
配套的应用程序实在令人失望。它的交互设计算不上顶尖——但你也能轻松上手。真正的问题在于频繁的崩溃以及录制视频时出现的掉帧现象。
由于镜头设计的原因，它并不适合用于寻找漏水点和热点等家庭任务。对于这类需求，你会需要像我上周评测过的 Hikmicro 设备那样的产品。
能够直接插到手机上意味着它可以轻松融入你的工作流程。你可以像往常一样编辑、裁剪和发布图像。对于这么小的设备来说，它能呈现的图像信息非常丰富——而且其板载处理能力十分出色。
遗憾的是，它的变焦是数字变焦，而不是光学变焦。你只是在放大像素，而不是真正靠近拍摄对象。
图像质量极其出色，但 Android 应用程序实在令人失望。如果你能忍受令人费解的界面和偶尔的崩溃，你就能用它拍出一些精美的照片和视频。

articles.title: Ebay’s 1995 debut
articles.summary: eBay 的域名于 1995 年 8 月 4 日注册，但网站直到同年 9 月 3 日才正式上线。该平台最初并不叫 eBay，而是以 Auctionweb 的名字首次亮相。文章回顾了这家电商巨头在 31 年前的早期发展历程，揭示了其品牌演变的历史细节。结论是，许多互联网巨头在初创时期都经历过名称和定位的调整。
articles.summaryEn: The eBay domain name was registered on August 4, 1995, but the site did not officially launch until September 3 of the same year. The platform originally debuted under the name Auctionweb rather than eBay. The article reviews the early development history of this e-commerce giant 31 years ago, revealing historical details of its brand evolution. Many internet giants experienced adjustments in naming and positioning during their initial stages.

blocks.text: The eBay domain name was registered 31 years ago today, on August 4, 1995. But the site we know today as Ebay didn’t launch until almost month later, September 3, 1995, under a different name. Auctionweb, the original name for Ebay, was a side project. From these humble beginnings came one of the few survivors of the dotcom era.
What the Ebay name meant

The name eBay was always a little bit curious. Other early online auction sites had the word “auction” in the name, or at least something related to selling. I made my first few online auction purchases from a site called onsale.com. Sticking the letter “e” in front of whatever you were selling and registering a dotcom was a common tactic in the late 90s.
But a bay? That’s a body of water. Sure, bays are convenient places for ships to dock so the name kinda-sorta evokes trading, but it doesn’t seem like the best name for an auction site.

Originally it wasn’t. Originally Ebay stood for Echo Bay Technology Group, Pierre Omidyar’s other company. Auction Web was his side project. With echobay.com already taken by a gold mining company, he shortened it to Ebay.
From Auctionweb to Ebay

The story that Pierre Omidyar started Auction Web to help his finacee sell Pez dispensers is apocryphal. It was a hobby project over Labor Day weekend to help him make some extra money by selling stuff he didn’t need, like a broken laser pointer he sold for $14.83. By February, he was getting so much traffic his ISP informed him he was ineligible to use a $30 personal account, he’d have to upgrade to a business account priced at $250 per month. This proved fortuitious, as it drove Omidyar to start charging for use. He turned a $1,000 profit in his first month and a $2,500 profit his second. Within 14 months, the young site had hosted more than 200,000 auctions.

Auctionweb changed its name in September 1997. Short domain names gained more traffic because they were easier to type, and Omidyar already owned the ebay.com domain name. I remember winning some auctions for used computer parts in the fall of 1998 on Ebay, including the floppy drive that’s now in my IBM 5170, but I don’t remember anymore how I found out about the site.

The same year, Ebay received $6.7 million in venture capital funding. The most popular items on the site were Beanie Babies. Ebay had a more user friendly interface than the official site for trading Beanie Babies, making it popular with Beanie Baby collectors and toy collectors in general.

In September 1998, Ebay held its IPO at $18 per share, reaching $53 per share in its first day, making Omidyar and Jeffrey Skoll, Ebay’s first president, instant billionaires. Ebay’s first annual report listed the company’s dependence on the continued strength of the Beanie Baby market as a risk factor.
Surviving the dotcom bust

Even before the dotcom bust, Ebay was widely considered one of the four safest dotcom investments, alongside Amazon, AOL, and Yahoo. Ebay didn’t end up as big as Amazon, and it didn’t rise to the heights AOL did, but it didn’t fall like AOL or Yahoo either. In 2024, it had $10 billion in revenue and $1.98 billion in profits, against $5.16 billion in equity and $19.4 billion in total assets. It employed 11,500 people.

In 2003, Fortune listed Ebay as the 8th fastest growing company. By 2006, it had cracked the Fortune 500, landing at number 458. Ebay’s growth paralleled the growth of the Internet, so Ebay lost its shine as the number of new Internet subscribers tailed off, bringing down the number of new Ebay users along with it. But its status as a dotcom survivor makes it a rare bird. It didn’t eclipse Microsoft in size like Amazon or Google did, but reaching the Fortune 500 and maintaining a position on it is an achievement not many other dotcoms attained.

David Farquhar is a computer security professional, entrepreneur, and author. He has written professionally about computers since 1991, so he was writing about retro computers when they were still new. He has been working in IT professionally since 1994 and has specialized in vulnerability management since 2013. He holds Security+ and CISSP certifications. Today he blogs five times a week, mostly about retro computers and retro gaming covering the time period from 1975 to 2000.

translations: 就在31年前的今天，即1995年8月4日，eBay域名被注册。但我们今天熟知的Ebay网站直到近一个月后的1995年9月3日才上线，而且当时用的是另一个名字。Auctionweb是Ebay最初的名字，它只是一个业余项目。正是从这些不起眼的起点，诞生了互联网泡沫时代为数不多的幸存者之一。
Ebay这个名字的含义
eBay这个名字总是让人有点好奇。其他早期的在线拍卖网站名字里都有“auction”这个词，或者至少有与销售相关的字眼。我最初几次在线拍卖购物是在一个叫onsale.com的网站上进行的。在90年代末，在你要卖的东西前面加上字母“e”并注册一个.com域名是一种常见的策略。
但是bay（海湾）呢？那是一片水域。当然，海湾是船只停靠的便利场所，所以这个名字多少能让人联想到贸易，但它似乎并不是拍卖网站的最佳名字。
最初确实不是。Ebay最初代表Echo Bay Technology Group，这是皮埃尔·奥米迪亚的另一家公司。Auction Web只是他的业余项目。由于echobay.com已经被一家金矿公司注册，他将其缩短为Ebay。
从Auctionweb到Ebay

关于皮埃尔·奥米迪亚为了帮助未婚妻出售Pez糖果盒而创办Auction Web的故事是虚构的。那是他在劳工节周末的一个业余项目，旨在通过出售不需要的物品来赚点外快，比如他以14.83美元卖掉的一个坏掉的激光笔。到了2月份，网站的流量激增，以至于他的ISP通知他不能再使用30美元的个人账户，必须升级到每月250美元的商业账户。这反而成了件幸运的事，因为它促使奥米迪亚开始对网站的使用收费。他在第一个月就获得了1000美元的利润，第二个月利润达到2500美元。在14个月内，这个年轻的网站已经举办了超过20万次拍卖。
Auctionweb在1997年9月更改了名称。简短的域名能带来更多流量，因为它们更容易输入，而且奥米迪亚已经拥有了ebay.com这个域名。我记得在1998年秋天，我在Ebay上竞拍到了一些二手电脑配件，包括现在装在我的IBM 5170里的那个软驱，但我已经不记得当时是怎么发现这个网站的了。
同年，Ebay获得了670万美元的风险投资。网站上最受欢迎的商品是豆豆公仔（Beanie Babies）。Ebay的界面比交易豆豆公仔的官方网站更加用户友好，这使其在豆豆公仔收藏家和整个玩具收藏界都大受欢迎。
1998年9月，Ebay以每股18美元的价格进行了IPO，首日股价便达到每股53美元，使奥米迪亚和Ebay首任总裁杰弗里·斯科尔瞬间成为亿万富翁。Ebay的第一份年度报告将公司对豆豆公仔市场持续强劲的依赖列为风险因素。
在互联网泡沫中幸存
甚至在互联网泡沫破裂之前，Ebay就被广泛认为是最安全的四大互联网投资之一，与Amazon、AOL和Yahoo齐名。Ebay最终没有像Amazon那样庞大，也没有达到AOL曾经的高度，但它也没有像AOL或Yahoo那样衰落。2024年，它的收入为100亿美元，利润为19.8亿美元，权益为51.6亿美元，总资产为194亿美元。它雇佣了11,500名员工。

2003年，《财富》杂志将Ebay列为增长第八快的公司。到2006年，它成功跻身《财富》500强，位列第458位。Ebay的增长与互联网的发展同步，因此随着新增互联网用户数量的减少，Ebay也失去了往日的光芒，新增Ebay用户数量也随之下降。但作为互联网泡沫的幸存者，它的地位使其显得尤为罕见。虽然它的规模没有像Amazon或Google那样超越Microsoft，但能够进入并保持在《财富》500强榜单上，是许多其他互联网公司未能企及的成就。
David Farquhar 是一名计算机安全专家、企业家和作家。他从1991年开始从事专业的计算机写作，因此当复古计算机还是新鲜事物时，他就在撰写关于它们的文章。他从1994年开始从事专业的IT工作，并自2013年起专注于漏洞管理。他拥有 Security+ 和 CISSP 认证。如今他每周写五篇博客，主要探讨1975年至2000年间的复古计算机和复古游戏。
